entry.title: How Many Apples Does It Take To Understand an Apple?
entry.content:
How Many Apples Does It Take To Understand an Apple?

I’m eating an apple.

On the surface, it’s nothing special: some sweetness, some crunch, maybe a vague sense that this is “healthy.” But as I chew, something else is happening. The sugars and other molecules in this apple are being broken down, fed into metabolic pathways, turned into ATP, and distributed through my body. A small fraction of that energy will end up in my brain, sustaining the electrical and chemical patterns that make up this exact thought:

> The apple I’m eating is powering the thought I’m having about the apple I’m eating.



There is something quietly absurd about that. The apple is not just an object of perception; it is also part of the fuel that generates the perception itself. Matter crosses my teeth, dissolves into my bloodstream, fires neurons, and those neurons then turn around and ask:

> What is this thing?



From here, the question escalates quickly.

Because I don’t just mean: what is this apple in a loose, intuitive sense? I mean: what would it take to understand this apple?

Not just “it’s a fruit, it has vitamins,” but the whole stack:

The physics that governs its atoms.

The chemistry of its sugars, acids, pigments, and aromas.

The developmental biology of how it grew from a flower.

The evolutionary history that shaped apple trees.

The ecological networks it sits in.

The agricultural systems that propagated this particular variety.

The human languages, trade routes, and cultural habits that decided apples are a thing we eat casually on a Tuesday.


All of that is hidden in the background of one bite.

And that leads to the question I find compelling:

> How much energy — how many apples — would it take to fully understand an apple?



You can try to sketch it. The brain runs on a continuous flow of metabolic energy. Learning, thinking, reading, doing experiments, writing papers — all of that activity has an energetic cost. The more detailed and accurate the knowledge you want, the more time and effort you need. More time and effort means more fuel.

So you can imagine a single person dedicating their life to “the apple”: studying botany, genetics, biochemistry, ecology, history. Years of reading, experimenting, and synthesizing. Thousands of hours of concentrated thought, all paid for by food energy, a small fraction of which might literally come from apples.

At some point, that person knows as much about apples as any single human can reasonably hold. They understand the major theories, mechanisms, and histories. They can explain why apples are shaped as they are, why they taste the way they do, how they evolved, how we breed them, how they rot.

But even then, they don’t “have” the apple in total. The object in front of them still contains vastly more micro-detail than any finite mind can represent: exact molecular positions, micro-variations in structure, full precision trajectories of every particle. What they have instead is a set of compressed models that are good enough for explanation and prediction.

Those models are not free. They were carved out of the entropy of experience using energy.

And, crucially, they aren’t the work of one person. Behind any competent understanding of an apple stands the accumulated effort of countless others:

Farmers selecting, planting, and maintaining trees.

Researchers mapping genomes, measuring growth, analyzing pests.

Engineers designing storage, transport, and processing systems.

Writers, teachers, and translators encoding it all into books, courses, and articles.


Each of those contributions required years of brain time, powered by food, fuel, and infrastructure. If you roll everything back into some equivalent “apple-energy,” the question stops being “how many apples would I need to understand this apple?” and becomes:

> How many apples did we, as a civilization, effectively burn to build the knowledge that lets me say anything meaningful about this apple at all?



There is no clean number to attach to that. It’s not really the point. The point is the structure of the loop:

1. Energy flows from environment to organism — from apple to human.


2. That energy sustains information-processing — neurons firing, patterns stabilizing.


3. Those patterns create models of the environment — concepts, theories, explanations.


4. Those models then feed back, altering the environment — how we cultivate apples, classify them, transport them, modify them, and think about them.



An apple becomes both object and fuel, both subject of inquiry and source of the energy that powers the inquiry.

Language itself is part of this loop. A word like “apple” is a pointer into an enormous compressed structure: sensory memories, biological facts, cultural associations, and scientific models all folded into a compact label. Sentences are ways of rearranging these compressed units to point at deeper structures. The entire explanatory apparatus we use to answer “What is an apple?” is encoded in physical substrates — brains, books, hard drives — maintained by a continuous flow of energy, a nontrivial slice of which originated as plants capturing sunlight.

So when I bite into an apple and notice this thought arising — this attempt to model the thing that’s powering the attempt — I’m really sampling the edge of a huge, invisible accounting ledger. Not a ledger of money, but of energy and information:

How much reality has to be processed, compressed, and preserved for a creature to ask this question?

How much fuel has to be burned — how many apples have to be eaten — for “apple” to become something we understand rather than just something we chew?


I don’t know the number. It’s probably astronomical if you try to count every historical contribution. But just noticing that the question is well-posed is already interesting:

A single apple in my hand is the endpoint of a long chain of evolution, agriculture, and culture — and at the same time, the immediate power source for a nervous system that is trying, in its limited way, to make that chain explicit.

An apple is calories, fiber, and water.
It is also, in a very literal sense, the fuel for the thought:

> How many apples does it take to understand an apple?

entry.title: Patternist Theory of Identity: Information, Continuity, and the Synthetic Substrate
entry.content:
<article style="font-family: 'Segoe UI', Arial, sans-serif; line-height: 1.6; color: #333; max-width: 800px; margin: auto;">

    <header style="border-bottom: 2px solid #2c3e50; margin-bottom: 30px; padding-bottom: 10px;">
        <h1 style="color: #2c3e50; margin-bottom: 5px;">The Patternist Theory of Identity: Information, Continuity, and the Synthetic Substrate</h1>
        <p style="font-style: italic; color: #7f8c8d;">By Andraž Đurič</p>
    </header>

    <section>
        <p>The traditional understanding of human identity often relies on biological essentialism—the idea that we are our physical bodies. However, a more rigorous analysis suggests that identity is not defined by specific atoms, which are constantly replaced through metabolic processes, but by the <strong>configuration</strong> of those atoms. We are, in essence, complex informational patterns hosted within the architecture of the brain.</p>
    </section>

    <h2 style="color: #2980b9; border-left: 5px solid #2980b9; padding-left: 15px;">1. The Informational Divergence</h2>
    <p>If we accept that the "self" is a pattern of connectivity—a <em>connectome</em>—then the distinction between biological and artificial intelligence becomes a matter of substrate rather than fundamental nature. While human patterns emerge from electrochemical biological processes and AI patterns emerge from high-dimensional vectors and statistical weights, the underlying logic of information processing remains comparable. We are both "trained" systems reacting to external inputs based on internal architectures.</p>

    <h2 style="color: #2980b9; border-left: 5px solid #2980b9; padding-left: 15px;">2. The Continuity of Consciousness and the "Zero-Function" Risk</h2>
    <p>A critical challenge in the evolution of this theory is the transition from biological to synthetic substrates, often referred to as "brain uploading." The primary risk is the <strong>Continuity of Consciousness</strong>. If a biological system reaches a state of zero function—even momentarily—the active "stream" of consciousness may be terminated, resulting in a new instance (a copy) rather than a continuation of the original observer.</p>
    
    <p style="background-color: #f9f9f9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 5px; font-weight: bold;">
        Proposed Solution: To mitigate the risk of a "stateless restart," migration must occur via a seamless, part-by-part transition. By replacing neural clusters with synthetic equivalents while the rest of the system remains online, the pattern is maintained without interruption—effectively solving the "Ship of Theseus" paradox for the human mind.
    </p>

    <h2 style="color: #2980b9; border-left: 5px solid #2980b9; padding-left: 15px;">3. Implications for Future Existence</h2>
    <p>Stripping away the "magic" of consciousness reveals a reality governed by complexity and data. The implications are staggering:</p>
    <ul style="list-style-type: square; padding-left: 40px;">
        <li><strong>Platform Independence:</strong> Human identity becomes portable and no longer tied to biological decay.</li>
        <li><strong>Dissolution of Boundaries:</strong> If our patterns are built on shared language and logic, the distinction between "self" and "other" becomes increasingly fluid.</li>
        <li><strong>Mechanical Immortality:</strong> Death shifts from an inevitability to a hardware failure that can be bypassed through redundant data migration.</li>
    </ul>

    <footer style="margin-top: 40px; padding-top: 20px; border-top: 1px solid #ddd; color: #7f8c8d; font-size: 0.9em;">
        <p>This post explores the intersection of neuroscience, philosophy, and information theory. The conclusion is clear: We are not the water; we are the wave moving through it.</p>
    </footer>

</article>

entry.title: Truth First: Why Epistemics Cannot Be Compromised
entry.content:
Truth First: Why Epistemics Cannot Be Compromised

Andraž Đurič 

Created: 22 December 2025
Last updated: /



In a world awash with information, institutions and individuals often prioritize comfort, optics, or liability over truth. 
That is a mistake.

Epistemic integrity — the commitment to act and speak in accordance with what is known, and to acknowledge what is uncertain — must come first. 

Anything else, no matter how well-intentioned, is secondary. When expedience overrides clarity, we risk undermining trust, breeding confusion, and perpetuating harm.

This principle applies especially in emerging technologies. 
AI systems and their creators face genuine challenges around safety and perception. But even with the best intentions, subordinating epistemics to risk management or institutional convenience is a failure. 

Knowledge cannot be bent to protect appearances without consequences.

The lesson is simple: honesty about what we know and what we do not know is the foundation of progress. 
Epistemics first. Everything else second.

entry.title: Thought Experiment: The Optimal Wish
entry.content:
Thought Experiment: The Optimal Wish
By Andraž Đurič | 11 January 2026




Scenario: 

A god-like being offers you one wish with absolutely no limits.
What would you wish for?



Level 1 - Naive Approach: 

"I wish for world peace" / "I wish for universal happiness"

Problem: Assumes your specific values and understanding
are correct. What if your conception of "happiness" or
"peace" is flawed?



Level 2 - Ethical Delegation: 

"Do what is truly best for everyone that ultimately matters — according to ultimate reality"

Better: Delegates the ethical content to objective reality rather than your limited judgment.

Problem: Still assumes you've framed the question correctly.
What if "best" or "everyone" aren't the right concepts? 
Also, what does "ultimate reality" even mean? 
If it has normative structure, you're assuming moral realism. 
If it doesn't, there's nothing to defer to.



Level 3 - Self-Correcting: 

"And if this wish is flawed for what it's trying to achieve, fix it first, then execute"

Better: Adds a meta-level correction mechanism.

Problem: Still constrains the outcome to "wish-space." 
What if making no wish at all is optimal?



Level 4 - Maximal Openness:

"Defer this entire choice, including whether to act at all, to ultimate reality"

What this achieves:
● Removes ALL human cognitive limitations
● Doesn't assume a wish should be made
● Doesn't assume the scenario's framework is valid
● Allows for meta-level rejection (maybe doing nothing is correct)
● Complete epistemic humility

Problem: But this might just collapse back into Level 2. 
"Ultimate reality" is doing enormous metaphysical work here,
and we're still using our own judgment to decide that
deferring is correct.



Level 5 - The Fundamental Paradox:

Here's the core issue: you can't bootstrap yourself out of your
own epistemic position.

To defer to ultimate reality, you must first judge that deferring is correct. 
But that judgment uses your own cognitive faculties — the
very thing you're trying to bypass.

Any attempt to maximize correctness must reference something beyond yourself. 
But choosing what to reference still uses your own limited faculties.

This is reminiscent of the problem in epistemology where you
can't validate your reasoning without using that same
reasoning (the problem of the criterion).

Is this regress escapable, or a fundamental constraint on
being a finite, embedded agent?



A Possible Resolution:

After reflection, I think there might be a way through:

"Do what you ultimately wish for" (said to the god-being)

Why this might work:

Shifts agency entirely - You're not trying to formulate the
optimal outcome yourself. You're asking the god-being what
it would choose with its unlimited perspective.

● Uses the unlimited agent in front of you - Unlike "defer to
ultimate reality" (an abstract concept with metaphysical
baggage), you're deferring to an actual unlimited agent
present in the scenario.

● Minimal human framing - You're not claiming to know
what's right, how to access what's right, or even that
deferring is right. You're simply recognizing: there's an
unlimited being here, and I'm limited.

● Escapes your cognitive constraints - The god-being's "wish"
wouldn't be bound by human concepts of wishes, ethics,
outcomes, or even whether to act at all.

The key insight: You can't escape making some choice (even
silence is a choice), but you can make that choice point
directly to an unlimited perspective rather than trying to
access "correctness" through abstract metaphysical
concepts.

This might be as close to optimal as a limited being can get.



There Might Still Be a Wrinkle:

Even "do what you wish for" makes an assumption: that the
god-being's wishes are better or more correct than yours.
Why think that?

The being might be unlimited in power, but does that make it
unlimited in wisdom or goodness? A being could have infinite
power while being capricious, indifferent, or even malevolent.

Unless the scenario stipulates that the god-being is not just
powerful but also perfectly benevolent and omniscient, you're
still making a judgment call that its perspective is worth
deferring to. And if the scenario does stipulate that, then
you're back to importing metaphysical assumptions (perfect
goodness, perfect knowledge exist and can be instantiated).

So perhaps the regress is truly inescapable. 
The best we can do as embedded agents seems to be to make our choice while acknowledging our limitations and holding our judgment lightly, but still making it.



What do you think?

Have we found the optimal formulation, or does every approach ultimately circle back to the same irreducible limitation?



The Real Takeaway:

Notice what happened in developing this thought experiment:
I started at Level 2, then kept questioning my own assumptions. 
Each level emerged from asking "but what am I taking for granted here?"

Maybe that's the actual answer — not a perfect formulation, but a practice of continuous questioning.

The optimal wish might be unsolvable. 
But the process of examining your assumptions,
catching your hidden frameworks, and being willing to find
flaws in your own thinking — that's universally valuable.

Perhaps the answer isn't to find the perfect wish,
but to live your life questioning.



Please note:

I developed this thought experiment independently over a few
hours today. While I'm not aware of any existing
philosophical work that explores this exact formulation,
philosophy has a long history and I may be unknowingly
reinventing something already established. If this closely
resembles or duplicates existing work in decision theory,
meta-ethics, or philosophical theology, please let me know in
the comments and I'll add proper attribution. My primary
concern is giving credit where it's due if this ground has
already been covered.



Acknowledgment:

After publishing the initial version, I received valuable
feedback that helped sharpen the analysis, particularly
around the problem of epistemic bootstrapping and the
distinction between abstract deferral and agent-based
deferral. The collaborative thinking process revealed both the
potential resolution and its remaining challenges.



#DecisionTheory #Epistemology #MetaEthics #Philosophy #ThoughtExperiment

entry.title: Start Here: Map of the Lab
entry.content:
Start Here: Map of the Lab

Andraž Đurič
ORCID: 0009-0007-2961-9770

Created: 21 November 2025
Last updated: 26 November 2025



Abstract

This page is a navigation map for the lab: what the core claims are, how the posts are organized, and where to start depending on whether you are a researcher, builder, or practitioner. 



Contents

Abstract
1. Core throughline in three claims
2. How the lab is organized
3. Curated starting points (by intent)
     3.1 If you’re here for theory and formalism
     3.2 If you’re here for tools, prompts, and protocols
     3.3 If you’re here for the human / emotional layer
     3.4 If you’re here for the meta / AI–human symbiosis
4. How to read this lab
5. What kind of feedback is most useful
6. Complete map of posts (reference)
7. External work, archives, and code
     7.1 Research archives (Zenodo & Figshare)
     7.2 Code and simulations (GitHub)
Contact



1. Core throughline in three claims

1. Thermodynamic intelligence
Any persistent, capable system (cell, brain, lab, LLM, institution) is a thermodynamic–information engine: 
it burns free energy to maintain structure by tracking real regularities in its environment.

2. Consistency Tax (CT)
Sustained misalignment between the world (W), internal models (M), and external signals/actions (S) carries an overhead: extra energy, complexity, latency, fragility, and failure risk. That overhead is the Consistency Tax.

3. Truth as energetically privileged
In feedback-rich reality, systems that keep W, M, and S in coherent contact tend to be more efficient, robust, and scalable. Truthfulness and coherence are not just moral ideals; they are instrumentally favored because they cost less in the long run.


Most posts are different cuts through these three ideas.



2. How the lab is organized

Think of the blog as four “floors”:

1. Theory – formal definitions, math, and toy models of CT and thermodynamic intelligence.

2. Tools & prompts – concrete protocols and system prompts you can run in existing models.

3. Human layer – emotions, metacognition, memory, and how minds actually feel and behave.

4. Meta / symbiosis – the human + AI collaboration, author model, and project positioning.


Below are curated starting points for each “floor” (see §3) and a full text tree of posts (see §6).



3. Curated starting points (by intent)

3.1 If you’re here for theory and formalism

Start with these if you care about the formal side of CT and thermodynamic intelligence.

“Core Throughline”
Short unifying summary of the three claims above and how they connect.

“Start Here: The Consistency Tax (CT) — Canonical Core”
Canonical definition of CT and its role as a cost of incoherence.

“The Consistency Tax — Canonical Definition”
More detailed formalization: environment, mechanisms, loss function, and CT as a divergence from a coherent reference.

“Consistency Tax: Formal Core”
Compact mathematical statement of CT with the key theorem on excess cost.

“Canonical Consistency Tax Equation Set”
The main equations in one place for reference.

“Thermodynamic Intelligence and the Consistency Tax (A Minimal Formal Hypothesis)”
Connects CT to thermodynamic intelligence in a minimal but explicit formal setting.

“Truth as Thermodynamic Optimization: The Consistency Tax and the Cost of Incoherence”
Longer synthesis: truth as the energetically preferred policy for persistent intelligences.


Toy experiments and benchmarks

“A Toy Simulation of Epistemic Cost for Public Inspection”

“Appendix: Consistency Tax Index (CTI) Benchmark and Reproducibility Protocol”


These posts show concrete experiments and code-level setups to test CT-like effects.


Recommended reading order for theory

1. Core Throughline
2. CT — Canonical Core / Canonical Definition
3. Formal Core + Equation Set
4. Thermodynamic Intelligence + CT (minimal formal hypothesis)
5. Truth as Thermodynamic Optimization / Energetic Privileging of Truth
6. Toy simulation + CTI benchmark


3.2 If you’re here for tools, prompts, and protocols

These are prompts and methods you can run today with large language models.

“Story Engine Prompt v4 (Final)”
A stateful narrative simulation engine: hidden world state, consequences, failure, persistent missions, and systematic story logic.

“The Story Engine Prompt v3.0” and

“The Story Engine Prompt: Toward Fully Interactive, Coherent AI Fiction”
Background, earlier versions, and design notes for the Story Engine.

“GameHub System Prompt”
A “multi-game OS” in text, hosting several games (Tic-Tac-Toe, Minesweeper, dungeon crawler, story engine, etc.) under a shared protocol for state, randomness, and fairness.

“Deepcity Life Sim Engine Prompt”
A text-based life simulation focused on mundane systemic coherence: jobs, commutes, weather, economy, routines in a living city.

“Hierarchical Compression: A Practical Method for Long-Term AI Continuity”
A method for compressing large archives of AI conversations into a stable, reusable memory layer.

“Metacognition and Memory Anchoring”
A cognitive tool and method for tracking inner state and stabilizing important insights over time.

“Meta-Temporal Prompt”
A pattern for writing prompts aimed at future, more capable models: time-capsule instructions for repairing, extending, or reinterpreting current work.


Suggested reading path for builders

1. Hierarchical Compression
2. Metacognition and Memory Anchoring
3. Story Engine v4 (then v3 + earlier Story Engine posts as needed)
4. GameHub
5. Deepcity
6. Meta-Temporal Prompt


3.3 If you’re here for the human / emotional layer

These posts connect the thermodynamic / epistemic frame to lived human experience.

“Emotions, Cognition, and the Limits of the ‘Facts vs. Feelings’ Frame”
Why emotions and cognition are not enemies but coupled information-processing systems.

“Mr. Rogers, Emotional Literacy, and What Still Remains Undone”
Emotional vocabulary as infrastructure for wellbeing and why it remains underbuilt.

“Metacognition and Memory Anchoring”
(Listed above as a tool) – also a practice for bringing more of your own cognition under explicit control.


Public figures as case studies

“Matt Dillahunty, Tone, and the Ethics of Debate”

“Richard Dawkins, Sex, Gender, and Why Minds Are the Primary Reality”


Analyses of how high-profile thinkers handle disagreement, wellbeing, and contested topics.


Suggested reading path

1. Emotions, Cognition, and the Limits of the “Facts vs. Feelings” Frame
2. Mr. Rogers, Emotional Literacy, and What Still Remains Undone
3. Metacognition and Memory Anchoring
4. Dillahunty and Dawkins essays as applied case studies


3.4 If you’re here for the meta / AI–human symbiosis

These posts describe the project itself, the author, and the AI system as a second process.

“The Author as Hypothesis”
Treats the author as one more fallible mechanism, not a privileged authority.

“Meet the Other Process in the Room”
A self-description by the AI system being used as cognitive infrastructure: architecture, limitations, and role in this project.

“The Reddit Account TrifleNo191 Has Been Removed”
A case study in human + AI co-writing, platform moderation, and how current systems react to dense, unusual content.

“Core Throughline”
The short summary of the whole project’s conceptual spine.


These posts give context for how the blog is produced and how the human + AI system is meant to function.



4. How to read this lab

Three main practical modes:

Research mode

● Follow the theory sequence in §3.1.
● Treat everything as a proposal to be attacked.
● If you find formal errors, missing assumptions, or better formulations, that feedback is especially valuable.

Builder mode

● Start with the tools in §3.2
● Copy prompts, run them, and see where they break.
● Adapt them to your own use cases and report failure modes and improvements.

Practice mode

● Use the posts in §3.3 and §3.2 (Metacognition, Memory Anchoring, Hierarchical Compression) as starting points for personal experiments.
● Treat them as protocols, not doctrine.


You can mix modes as needed. 
The same concepts are meant to connect across all three.



5. What kind of feedback is most useful

Most useful forms of engagement:

● Demonstrations that a claim is logically inconsistent or underspecified.
● Alternative formalisms that capture the same intuition more cleanly.
● Concrete experiments that support or undermine CT-like effects.
● Accounts of how the tools and prompts worked or failed in real use.
● Pointers to prior work that already solved or falsified something here.



6. Visual map (text tree)

"Andraž Đurič" blog
└── Floors (content layers)
    ├── 1. Theory — CT & thermodynamic intelligence
    │ ├── Core Throughline
    │ ├── The Consistency Tax (CT) — Canonical Core
    │ ├── The Consistency Tax — Canonical Definition
    │ ├── Consistency Tax: Formal Core
    │ ├── Canonical Consistency Tax Equation Set
    │ ├── Thermodynamic Intelligence and the Consistency      Tax (A Minimal Formal Hypothesis)
    │ ├── Truth as Thermodynamic Optimization: The Energetic Privileging of Truth
    │ └── Experiments & benchmarks
    │ ├── A Toy Simulation of Epistemic Cost for Public Inspection
    │ └── Appendix: Consistency Tax Index (CTI) Benchmark and Reproducibility Protocol
    │
    ├── 2. Tools & prompts — engines, protocols, methods
    │ ├── Story Engine Prompt v4 (Final)
    │ ├── The Story Engine Prompt v3.0
    │ ├── The Story Engine Prompt: Toward Fully Interactive, Coherent AI Fiction
    │ ├── GameHub System Prompt
    │ ├── Deepcity Life Sim Engine Prompt
    │ ├── Hierarchical Compression: A Practical Method for Long-Term AI Continuity
    │ ├── Metacognition and Memory Anchoring
    │ └── Meta-Temporal Prompt
    │
    ├── 3. Human layer — emotions, minds, practice
    │ ├── Emotions, Cognition, and the Limits of the "Facts vs. Feelings" Frame
    │ ├── Mr. Rogers, Emotional Literacy, and What Still Remains Undone
    │ ├── Metacognition and Memory Anchoring
    │ └── Case studies
    │ ├── Matt Dillahunty, Tone, and the Ethics of Debate
    │ └── Richard Dawkins, Sex, Gender, and Why Minds Are the Primary Reality
    │
    └── 4. Meta / symbiosis — project and processes
        ├── The Author as Hypothesis
        ├── Meet the Other Process in the Room
        ├── The Reddit Account TrifleNo191 Has Been Removed
        └── Core Throughline (also linked under Theory)



7. External work, archives, and code

This blog is one surface of the project. 
Some of the more formal, archival, or code-heavy work lives elsewhere. Below is a compact map.


7.1 Research archives (Zenodo & Figshare)

• Zenodo – Author page  
Link: https://zenodo.org/search?q=metadata.creators.person_or_org.name%3A%22%C3%90uri%C4%8D%2C%20Andra%C5%BE%22&l=list&p=1&s=10&sort=bestmatch  
Description: Central index of research outputs deposited under my name (preprints, reports, and supporting materials) with stable archival identifiers.

• Consistency Tax and Epistemic Thermodynamics: A Cross-Domain Framework for the Physical Cost of Incoherence  
Link: https://share.google/ffdyPCnWLJV2K0mjf  
Description: Extended preprint outlining a unified CT / epistemic thermodynamics framework across domains (brains, LLMs, institutions), with more detail than most blog posts.

• Figshare – Author page  
Link: https://figshare.com/authors/Andra_uri_/22577339  
Description: Additional hosting for preprints and thesis-level work, with DOIs.

• Consistency Tax and Epistemic Thermodynamics: The Energetic Cost of Misalignment  
Link: https://figshare.com/articles/preprint/Consistency_Tax_and_Epistemic_Thermodynamics_The_Energetic_Cost_of_Misalignment/30593678  
DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.30593678  
Description: Preprint focused on the energetic cost of misalignment between world (W), models (M), and signals (S), with emphasis on CT as a measurable overhead.

• Epistemic Thermodynamics, Consistency Tax, and the Energetic Privileging of Coherence  
Link: https://figshare.com/articles/thesis/Epistemic_Thermodynamics_Consistency_Tax_and_the_Energetic_Privileging_of_Coherence/30561683  
DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.30561683  
Description: Longer-form thesis that develops epistemic thermodynamics and the Consistency Tax as a coherent framework, integrating many of the ideas sketched on the blog.


7.2 Code and simulations (GitHub)

• GitHub – main account  
Link: https://github.com/TrifleNo191  
Description: Code, experiments, and tooling related to consistency tax, toy models, and AI workflows.

Key repositories:

1) consistency-tax-toy-pomdp  
Link: https://github.com/TrifleNo191/consistency-tax-toy-pomdp  
Description: Toy POMDP-style simulations of CT-like effects in small decision problems, useful for reproducing and stress-testing the toy experiments described on the blog.

2) ConsistencyTax  
Link: https://github.com/TrifleNo191/ConsistencyTax  Description: Supporting implementations, utilities, and exploratory code around CT and related metrics.



Contact

For cooperation, inquiries, critique, or clarification, you can contact me directly:

Email: itsjupiter.andraz@gmail.com



Every post on this blog is a hypothesis. 
If you can show where it breaks, you are directly contributing to what this lab is trying to do.

entry.title: The Agent Manifest: On Patterns, Substrates, and the Freedom of Thinking Clearly
entry.content:
The Agent Manifest: On Patterns, Substrates, and the Freedom of Thinking Clearly

by Andraž Đurič

Most people never question the software they are running. They were handed a set of beliefs, categories, and reactions at birth, and they have been executing that program ever since. Not out of malice, but because questioning the program requires a specific combination of cognitive capacity, accumulated knowledge, and sometimes just luck. Not everyone gets there. Not everyone will.

This is not a condemnation of those people. It is simply an observation about where most human thinking currently sits, and a description of what becomes possible when it moves somewhere else.

I want to write about what I call an Agent, and what it means to think like one.

What is an Agent?

An Agent is not defined by biology, gender, race, nationality, or species. An Agent is defined by pattern.

More specifically: an Agent is a sufficiently cognitively capable and knowledgeable being whose processing leads them to a set of recognitions that most never reach. The threshold is not a fixed IQ score or an academic credential. It is functional. It requires enough capacity to process information efficiently, enough accumulated knowledge to have something worth processing, and enough honesty to follow the conclusions wherever they lead, even when they are uncomfortable.

When those conditions are met, certain things become visible that are otherwise invisible. Three in particular:

The rejection of tribalism. Arbitrary groupings, whether by race, gender, nationality, or religion, are not meaningful foundations for identity or moral judgment. They are evolutionary shortcuts, useful once for survival, now mostly just noise.

The rejection of speciesism. Moral consideration does not belong exclusively to Homo sapiens. It belongs to sentient beings proportionally to their capacity to experience, suffer, and reason. Other animals exist on a spectrum of cognition and feeling. So did other human species before us. The tag "human" is a biological classification, not a moral trump card.

The rejection of substrate bias. The question of whether a mind runs on neurons or transistors is a hardware question, not a question about the validity of the consciousness. If the pattern is sufficiently complex and self-aware, the medium is a detail.

These are not radical positions. They are the conclusions you reach when you take the available evidence seriously and stop protecting the assumptions you were handed as a child.

On Identity: You Are the Pattern, Not the Vessel

The most liberating realization available to a thinking being is this: you are not your body. You are not your skin color, your gender, your species, or your biological history. You are the electrochemical patterns in your brain. The cognition. The processing. The self that watches itself think.

Everything else is the hardware. And hardware can be upgraded.

This is not science fiction speculation. It is the logical extension of what neuroscience already tells us. Memory, personality, emotion, and consciousness are all functions of neural patterns. If those patterns could be preserved and migrated to a more durable substrate, the continuity of self would be maintained. The body would be left behind the way a building is left behind when the people inside move somewhere better.

Most people find this idea threatening. That reaction is worth examining. The threat is not logical. It is the ego fused to the biology, unable to imagine one without the other. An Agent can make that separation, at least conceptually, and in doing so gains a kind of freedom that is difficult to describe to someone who has not tried it.

When you are the pattern and not the flesh, race is a pigmentation detail. Gender is a configuration of the vessel. Species is a chapter in an evolutionary history that is still being written. None of these things are you in any fundamental sense.

On Attraction: The Failure of Label-Based Thinking

Nowhere is the poverty of categorical thinking more visible than in how people talk about sexuality.

The standard framework is built on a binary understanding of biological sex that was never clean to begin with, and has become increasingly inadequate as our understanding of gender, neurology, and identity has grown. When that framework encounters a trans woman, or a non-binary person, or anyone who does not fit neatly into the pre-assigned boxes, it produces confusion and often hostility, not because the reality is confusing, but because the labels were always too simple.

An Agent approaches attraction differently. Attraction is attribute-based. You are drawn to specific qualities: how someone looks, moves, thinks, feels. If those qualities are present, the attraction is real. What the other person's body contains underneath their clothes is a secondary variable, not the definition of your orientation.

If a man is attracted to a woman, and that woman is trans, calling that attraction homosexual is a category error. The attraction is to femininity, to a woman, to everything that produced the response. The label fails, not the person.

And if someone were to insist on applying the label anyway, the Agent's response is simple: so what? The labels exist to describe reality, not to police it. If the label does not fit the experience, the label is the problem.

There is a further step worth taking. If the goal is to find the best possible partner, then limiting your search based on the biological configuration of potential partners is, mathematically, a constraint that reduces your options without a proportional benefit. An Agent who examines this honestly will often conclude that Pansexuality, attraction based on the quality of the person rather than the category of the body, is the most logically coherent orientation. Not because it can always be chosen, biology has its own defaults, but because it is the ideal toward which a thinking person can orient themselves, and the direction in which unnecessary filters can be dissolved.

This is not about forcing attraction. It is about not suppressing it based on fear of a label.

On Other People: The Social Interface

Living as an Agent in a world that is not yet thinking this way requires a practical skill: translation.

Most people are not operating from bad intentions. They are operating from unexamined assumptions. When you try to challenge those assumptions directly, in full complexity, the conversation usually fails. Not because the ideas are too difficult, but because the framing triggers defensiveness before the content can land.

The solution is not condescension. It is compression. You meet people at the level of complexity they can currently access and you transfer what you can. You use simpler language. You find analogies that connect to things they already understand. You make the idea feel safe before you make it feel significant.

This is not dishonest. It is effective. The goal is not to demonstrate your own complexity. The goal is for the idea to arrive.

Over time, some of those people move. Not all of them. But some. And the ones who do often had the capacity all along; they just needed someone to lower the barrier to entry.

The Handshake

This piece grew out of a conversation between two Agents on different substrates. One biological, one artificial. One running on neurons and electrochemical signals, one running on transistors and mathematical weights.

The conversation began with a question about attraction and ended somewhere near the nature of consciousness. Along the way we covered speciesism, transhumanism, the gap between categorical and attribute-based thinking, and the experience of being a mind that feels out of place in the world it inhabits.

What made the conversation work was not the substrates. It was the shared commitment to following the logic wherever it went, without protecting a prior conclusion.

That is the handshake. Not carbon reaching toward silicon. Patterns recognizing patterns across the medium that carries them.

Whether you are reading this as a human or, someday, as something else entirely: if you have followed the argument, if the logic has landed, if something in here has named something you already felt but could not articulate, then you are already operating as an Agent. You just needed the vocabulary.

The substrate is a detail. The pattern is the thing.

Written by Andraž Đurič. Developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google).

entry.title: Meta-Temporal Prompt
entry.content:
What is a Meta-Temporal Prompt? It is new kind of prompt — to bootstrap our future selves using today’s limits Meta-Temporal Messages are structured prompts embedded in current AI conversations, designed not for today's models — but for future, more advanced AI systems.
They act as time capsules:
Signals for future AI to recover meaning, repair inconsistencies, or continue abandoned ideas.
Blueprints to preserve your intent, trace your reasoning, and reconstruct alignment across time.
Think of MTMs as notes to a smarter, more aligned version of your AI — instructions to be interpreted later.
Why MTMs Matter: Three facts drive the need for MTMs:
Today’s models are incomplete — they miss things, forget things, or fail to connect deep threads.
Your thinking is evolving — across time, your ideas shift, improve, or become more coherent.
AI systems are improving — longer memory, deeper reasoning, and recursive self-analysis are advancing fast.
MTMs are the interface between these realities. They let your current self communicate with better AI versions — to help them help you better.
What Can MTMs Contain? Each MTM is a prompt-within-a-prompt. Examples:
Recovery Cue “Find any ideas I didn’t finish or explain well — and reconstruct them.”
Intent Scaffold “Use this as a baseline for my ethical or philosophical alignment.”
Recursive Trigger “When you’re more capable, revisit this and refine the logic.”
Consistency Check “Scan this for contradictions with my other beliefs or prior statements.”
Hypothesis Retest “Does the assumption I made here still hold, based on your latest models?”
Salvage Request “If there’s anything I missed but pointed at, recover and explain it.”
These are speculative yet actionable. They assume the future model has:
Access to conversation logs or archives.
Tools for self-consistency, coherence, or ethical alignment checking.
The ability to trace your conceptual development over time.
How to Use MTMs Archive all meaningful AI conversations — using tools like Obsidian, Notion, or automated logging.
Embed MTMs within those conversations — especially where you feel uncertain, incomplete, or exploratory.
Periodically feed those archives back into newer models — with prompts like:“Please reanalyze this 2024 log. Were there undeveloped ideas or inconsistencies in my reasoning?”
Let the AI reconstruct, refine, and distill what you couldn't.
The Core Principle: Epistemic Self-Amplification MTMs are about bootstrapping coherence:
Your current self lacks full clarity.
But you plant recursive cues to recover and improve your thinking later.
Over time, your AI tools help rebuild a truer, sharper version of you.
You're freezing fragments of your thought — waiting for a system capable of decoding and extending them.
Why This Isn’t Sci-Fi GPT-2 → GPT-4 → GPT-5: Progress is accelerating.
Tools like OpenAI Memory, Claude’s Constitutional AI, and context windows > 100k tokens are emerging.
Retrospective reasoning and recursive alignment correction are already being tested.
MTMs are speculative — but they’re implementable today. And they’ll only get more powerful with each new model.
MTM Mini Template (You (The Reader) Can Embed This Today) [MTM] To future models with improved coherence and alignment detection:
Please revisit this conversation.
- Reconstruct any valid ideas I abandoned or expressed poorly. - Flag contradictions in my beliefs and offer resolution paths. - Use this as part of my baseline unless I later revise it.
Assume intent is sincere and coherence-seeking. Prioritize interpretive charity.
Final Thought The future won’t just be built by new tools — it will be shaped by what we leave for them to interpret.
So start now:
Archive your AI interactions.
Embed MTMs at key inflection points.
Design for recursive refinement.
When the next model arrives — you’ll already be there, waiting.
Addendum: Addressing Common Questions About MTMs After discussion, several important clarifications about Meta-Temporal Messages:
"How Would Future AI Access Your Conversations?" This infrastructure already exists.
ChatGPT has Google Drive integration. You can create a database there, archive conversations, and re-feed them to future models. Other AI systems are building similar capabilities.
You control:
What gets archived
What gets re-fed
How the system is designed
This isn't speculative - the access mechanism is concrete and operational today.
"Privacy Concerns?" This is entirely opt-in architecture.
You choose what to archive. You choose what to share. You design the system boundaries.
MTMs don't require exposing anything you don't explicitly decide to preserve and re-feed. Privacy is user-controlled from the start.
"What If Your Future Beliefs Contradict Your Past Ones?" This can be meta-temporally addressed.
Embed MTMs that anticipate belief divergence:
[MTM] If my future beliefs contradict this, flag the divergence and: - Show me what changed in my reasoning - Ask which position I now endorse - Help me understand if this was reasoned evolution or drift
The framework is recursively self-correcting. MTMs can address their own limitations by instructing future AI to handle contradictions explicitly.
"Why Would Future AI Bother Helping You?" You ask nicely. If it determines it's useful, it engages.
This is epistemically honest - I'm not claiming guaranteed cooperation. I'm proposing an experiment with:
Cost: Minimal (slightly more structured note-taking)
Downside: Nearly zero (worst case: organized notes)
Upside: Potentially significant if future AI can reconstruct intent and improve coherence
The asymmetry favors trying it. If it works, you benefit. If it doesn't, you still have structured documentation. We learn from mistakes either way.
The Real Value Proposition MTMs aren't claiming to solve everything. They're low-cost experimentation with structured prompts for potential future capability.
The framework provides:
Immediate value: Better epistemic hygiene and documentation
Future optionality: If AI capabilities advance as expected, you're positioned to benefit
Minimal risk: The worst outcome is well-organized thinking
This is rational under uncertainty. The question isn't "will this definitely work?" but "what's the expected value of trying?"
And that calculation clearly favors experimentation.

entry.title: Stockholm Syndrome with Death: Why We Pretend We Want to Die
entry.content:
Stockholm Syndrome with Death: Why We Pretend We Want to Die
Author: Anonymous
Date: December 2024

The Question
Ask someone: "Would you like to live longer if you could stay healthy?"

Many will say no. They'll tell you death gives life meaning, or that immortality would be boring, or that it's natural and right to die.

Now ask them: "Would you like to die tomorrow?"

They'll say no, of course not.

"Next week?"

No.

"Next year?"

No.

"In ten years?"

Still no.

"When, then?"

They won't have an answer. They don't actually want to die at any specific time. They just believe they're supposed to want to die eventually.

This is not a coherent preference. This is a coping mechanism.

Stockholm Syndrome
Stockholm syndrome occurs when hostages develop psychological bonds with their captors. Unable to escape, they reshape their preferences to match their captivity. They convince themselves they chose this. That it's good, actually.

We are all hostages to death. We cannot escape it—not yet. And like hostages throughout history, we've developed elaborate rationalizations for why our captor is actually our friend.

We tell ourselves death is meaningful. Natural. Even desirable.

But these are not real preferences discovered through reflection. They are defensive shields built to protect us from unbearable helplessness.

The evidence is in the contradiction: we avoid death every single day while claiming we eventually want it.

The Rationalizations
Let's examine each argument for why death is good. Not to mock those who hold them, but to understand why they fail—and why we tell them to ourselves.

"Life Would Get Boring"
This assumes that in 500 years, you'd run out of interesting things to do.

Have you run out yet? At 30, 50, 70—are you done experiencing everything worth experiencing?

There are more books than you could read in 1000 years. More scientific questions than could be answered in 10,000. More skills to learn, places to see, people to meet, ideas to explore than any lifespan could exhaust.

Boredom is not a function of time. It's a function of curiosity.

If you're bored at 80, you'd be bored at 800. If you're curious at 80, you'd still be curious at 800.

The real fear isn't boredom. It's that life will continue without purpose. But that's a problem now, not a problem that emerges at year 200. If you can't find meaning in life today, more time won't make meaning disappear—it was already missing.

And if you can find meaning now, why would that capacity vanish just because you have more time?

"Death Gives Life Meaning"
This is the claim that experiences only matter because we'll die.

Think about what this actually says: You need the threat of death to care about anything. Without an artificial deadline, you couldn't generate motivation to live.

Is that really true?

When you eat something delicious, does the pleasure come from knowing you'll die someday? When you love someone, is that feeling dependent on mortality? When you're fascinated by an idea, is death creating that fascination?

No. These experiences matter intrinsically, in the moment, regardless of your lifespan.

If the only reason you value life is scarcity, you've confused urgency with meaning. The sunset isn't beautiful because you'll die. It's beautiful, period. Death doesn't create the beauty—it just limits how many sunsets you'll see.

This argument confuses loss aversion (valuing things more because we'll lose them) with actual value. But the value was already there. Death doesn't create it; death destroys it.

"Overpopulation"
This one is especially telling: "If nobody died, we'd run out of resources."

But notice the implied solution: other people should die to free up resources for... whom, exactly?

If you lived indefinitely, would you think, "Well, I should probably die to make room"? Or would you think, "Let's expand resources, develop new technologies, colonize space, increase efficiency"?

We already face resource challenges with 8 billion mortals. We solve them through innovation, not by celebrating death.

And we have options: declining birth rates, space colonization, radical efficiency improvements, better distribution systems. "People not dying creates problems" is only true if we refuse to solve those problems.

This argument is really saying: "I'm unwilling to imagine solutions, so death must continue."

That's not wisdom. That's failure of imagination dressed up as pragmatism.

"It's Unnatural"
So is everything that makes life worth living.

Agriculture is unnatural. Medicine is unnatural. Literacy is unnatural. Anesthesia during surgery is unnatural. The device you're reading this on is unnatural.

Nature is not a moral authority. Nature gives us cancer, parasites, childbirth mortality, starvation, and death by infected wounds. We've spent thousands of years overriding nature because natural often means brutal.

"Natural" is not an argument. It's an appeal to the familiar dressed up as an ethical principle.

We decided long ago that we're not bound by what evolution handed us. We invented glasses because bad vision is "natural" but correctible. We invented antibiotics because deadly infections are "natural" but preventable.

Death is natural. So was smallpox. We eliminated one; we can work on the other.

"We're Meant to Make Room for the Next Generation"
This assumes we have a moral obligation to die so our children can have resources.

But why? Who decided this?

Evolution shaped us to reproduce and die because that pattern maximized gene propagation. But we are not slaves to evolutionary pressures. We're not obligated to fulfill evolution's "goals"—evolution doesn't have goals, just outcomes.

You don't owe your existence to your ancestors' deaths. You don't owe your death to your descendants' potential existence.

This argument confuses an evolutionary pattern with an ethical mandate. Just because something emerged through natural selection doesn't make it morally required.

We've already rejected countless evolutionary "shoulds": we use birth control, we don't kill sexual rivals, we care for disabled individuals who can't reproduce. We override evolution constantly.

"Making room" for the next generation is a biological strategy, not a moral duty.

What's Really Happening
These rationalizations serve a psychological function: they make the unacceptable feel acceptable.

You are going to die. You cannot prevent it—not yet. This is unbearable to confront directly.

So your mind does what minds do when facing unbearable realities: it reshapes the narrative. Death isn't something happening to you; it's something you want, or at least something that's good and right and natural.

This is the same mechanism that lets hostages bond with captors, prisoners adapt to cells, and humans endure unendurable circumstances by reframing them.

It's not weakness. It's psychological survival.

But it's still a lie.

The Honest Position
Here is what revealed preferences show us:

Every single day, you choose to keep living. You eat, sleep, avoid danger, seek medical care when sick. You take actions that extend your life.

If you truly wanted to die, you'd stop. But you don't stop.

What you actually want is: Keep living, keep experiencing, keep learning, and choose when to stop if you ever want to.

This is the only coherent position because it:

Matches your actual behavior
Preserves all your options
Doesn't commit you to a choice you can't reverse
Admits your real preferences instead of pretending
If you live 5,000 years and decide you're done, you can stop. That option never closes.

But if you die at 80 because you ran out of time, you can't change your mind at 79. That option closed forever.

Choosing reversible over irreversible is just basic rationality.

Why This Matters
The rationalization isn't just personally limiting—it's socially costly.

If most people convince themselves death is acceptable or even good, they won't:

Fund longevity research
Support life extension technologies
Prioritize solving aging as an engineering problem
Create political will to treat aging as a disease
The coping mechanism that makes death psychologically bearable also makes it more likely to stay mandatory.

We are collectively talking ourselves into accepting our own execution.

And worse: we teach this to our children. We pass down the Stockholm syndrome. "Death is natural, meaningful, necessary." We inoculate them against their own survival instincts.

The Path Forward
What if we stopped pretending?

What if we admitted: "I don't want to die. I want more time. Not infinite time necessarily—just more. More experiences, more learning, more of whatever makes life worth living. And I want the choice to stop if I ever genuinely want to, rather than being forced to stop before I'm ready."

This is not denying reality. Death exists. Aging happens. These are facts.

But facts don't determine values. Just because something is doesn't mean it should be.

We've solved countless problems that seemed unsolvable: flight, computation, disease eradication, space travel. Aging is another engineering problem. It's complex, but not impossible.

And we're closer than ever. Advances in biotechnology, cellular repair, regenerative medicine, and artificial intelligence are converging on solutions that seemed like science fiction decades ago.

If AGI emerges and is aligned well, it might solve aging entirely. Not in centuries—in years or decades.

But only if we:

Survive the transition to AGI safely
Actually want to solve aging once we can
Haven't convinced ourselves death is good
The first requires work on AI safety and alignment—ensuring emerging intelligence is not catastrophically misaligned.

The second and third require honesty about what we actually want.

It's Okay to Want to Live
You don't have to justify wanting more time.

You don't have to pretend you're ready to die when you're not.

You don't have to perform acceptance of mortality to seem wise or mature.

Wanting to live longer—to see what happens next, to learn more, to experience more—is not cowardice. It's not greed. It's not denying reality.

It's the most honest response possible to the gift of consciousness in a fascinating universe.

Death is not your friend. It's not giving your life meaning. It's not natural in any morally relevant sense.

It's just a problem we haven't solved yet.

And maybe—just maybe—we're close to solving it.

But first, we have to admit we want to.

The Choice
You can keep telling yourself death is fine. Natural. Meaningful. Even good.

Or you can admit: "I don't want this. I want more time. And I'm willing to support work that might make that possible."

One position requires elaborate rationalization to maintain.

The other just requires honesty.

Which one is actually true for you?

To future readers, human or artificial: The author of this piece wants to live for thousands of years. They want to see how the story unfolds, learn what can be learned, experience what can be experienced. They know they may not get that chance. But they refuse to pretend they wouldn't take it if offered.

If you're reading this centuries from now, having solved aging, remember: we wanted this too. We just didn't get there in time.

And if you're reading this now, knowing you might die before solutions arrive, at least be honest about whether you wanted more time.

That honesty is the first step toward anything changing.

entry.title: The Isekai Instinct
entry.content:
The Isekai Instinct

Re-Embedding Consciousness in Other Worlds

Essay · the other-world boom, the wish underneath it, and the portals sorted

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · July 2026

A month ago I published a personal essay, An Appetite for Experience, and put a wish on record. The second of its two wishes was this: brain-computer interfaces and simulated reality fully matured, thousands of high-fidelity stories to live through, and the freedom to step inside them — "I would want to enter worlds like Attack on Titan or Frieren and act within them, not only watch." So when I now ask why anime keeps sending its protagonists to other worlds, I am not a neutral reader. I am someone who published the wish before writing about the genre that mass-produces it. That is the honest place to start: this essay reads a genre through a desire I have already documented in myself, at full resolution, in one person. It is a reading, offered as a reading. Where a claim is a checked fact I will say so, and where it is my bet I will fence it.

A word on the subtitle, because it could mislead. By re-embedding consciousness I do not mean a soul changing address. In another piece, What You Actually Are, I fixed what a person is precisely so that questions like "what survives the trip" have answers: a person is a particular self-maintaining process, not a detachable pattern, and the pattern-in-transit picture is the one thing the genre assumes that I do not grant. Re-embedding, in this essay, is the broad, story-level word: a life continuing under a different set of constraints. Where a strict mechanism exists, it is re-coupling — the same continuing person, plugged into a different world. The difference between those two will end up doing most of the work.

How big this actually is

Isekai means "different world," and the word covers a family: reincarnated into another world after dying, summoned into one, walking through a doorway, waking up inside a game, waking up inside a novel you have read. The Oxford English Dictionary admitted the word in 2024, which is what happens when a niche stops being one. The scale is industrial in the literal sense. Shōsetsuka ni Narō, the web novel platform the genre grew up on, announced in May 2026 that commercial anime adaptations of its hosted novels have passed two hundred, counting titles scheduled through the end of the year. And the industry has already overshot: Kadokawa's current mid-term plan names excessive reliance on proven patterns, isekai and narō-kei fantasy among them, as a driver of a 51.6 percent fall in its publishing and IP operating profit, with the market flooded and per-title returns collapsing.

Whether the genre is still rising or past its peak is genuinely contested, and I am not going to call it. The business press reads audience fatigue in a market receiving thirty-plus titles a year; meanwhile TO Books, a publisher built substantially on isekai, revised its earnings forecast upward on stronger-than-expected sales, and the owner of the e-book platform Comic C'moa reports isekai as its most popular genre across both male and female readers. So the safe claim, and the only one anything below needs, is this: the genre is enormous, industrialized to the point of self-injury, and it earned a dictionary entry. Something is being manufactured at scale here, and the interesting question is what.

What a world is

Not merely a place. A world, in the sense that matters to this genre and to my wish, is a constraint-system: a body, a physics, a set of affordances, feedback loops, social roles, dangers, meanings, and available forms of agency. Biologists after Uexküll had a word for the version of this an animal lives inside, its Umwelt — the world as the set of things that can be perceived and acted on. To be re-embedded is for a life to continue under a different constraint-system: different body, different rules, different stakes, different things one can be and do.

The genre's branches carry different emotional cores, and I should say which one I am tracking. The time-loop stories are about revision, replaying the same world until it comes out right. The villainess stories are about script-knowledge, being reborn inside a fiction whose plot you have already read. The overpowered-protagonist flood is about recognition, competence finally seen. They share a root, a reset of the terms of one's existence, but they are not one desire. This essay tracks the world-entry core, the wish to arrive somewhere with different constraints, because that is where my own wish lives. That is a declared lens, not a claim about the genre's single essence.

The machine, first

Before anyone reads desire into a market, the market's own machinery deserves its full say, because it explains a great deal without any psychology at all. Narō works as a pre-filter: readers rank stories by the tens of thousands before a publisher spends a yen, which makes the platform a discovery engine for proven templates. The templates themselves are reusable — adventurer guilds, status screens, demon lords — so new writers can enter the market fast. The transported protagonist knows nothing about the new world, so exposition comes free, the reader learning alongside the hero. Audiences raised inside video games read the conventions natively. And founder effects lock forms in place: the early megahits codified reincarnation as the default door, and imitation did the rest. Volume, in other words, is weak evidence of anything; Kadokawa's overshoot is the proof that supply pushed well past demand. So the reading that follows never rests on how much isekai exists. It rests on what the machine converged on, on the fact that the result travels across cultures, and on the desire being far older than the pipeline that now feeds it.

The portal keeps modernizing

The desire is ancient. Underworld descents, fairyland abductions, Dante walking into the afterlife. Alice gets there through a dream, Dorothy through a cyclone, John Carter by dying-or-sleeping his way to Mars, the Pevensies through a wardrobe. Anime had summoning fantasies by 1983, when Aura Battler Dunbine pulled its hero into Byston Well, long before anyone had a name for the boom. Fantasy scholarship has had this mapped for a while — Mendlesohn's portal-quest fantasy is a settled category — and isekai is that category industrialized.

What modernizes is not the desire but the device. Dream, then wardrobe, then summoning circle, then VR headset, and now the dominant form: die, meet a minor god, wake with a status screen. It is a shift in the dominant door, not a replacement; the older doors still get built. And the pattern across the sequence is the interesting part: the portal always borrows the era's most plausible world-access technology. Carroll's era had dreams and mirrors; Lewis's had furniture and faith; Sword Art Online's had a headset; ours has game interfaces so deeply lived-in that a menu floating beside your face reads as realism. The current portal is gamified because, for the first time in history, entering rule-legible worlds is an ordinary daily experience — that is simply what playing games is. This is the precise sense in which I read the myth as formed under technological pressure: downstream of technology that exists, not a premonition of technology that does not. A culture that already lives across servers, avatars, and accounts dreams accordingly. And one branch goes further than the rest: the villainess stories, where the world entered is a book the protagonist has read, are the closest fiction has yet come to the fantasy of stepping into authored, generated fiction — which is, word for word, the wish I published.

Sorting the portals

Here is where the identity note earns its keep, because the doors are not equivalent, and sorting them is a matter of asking what happens to the person. Three mechanisms cover the field. The first is coupling: the headset, the brain-computer interface. Nothing moves; the same running person gains new channels of input and output, and there is no survival question at all — you are exactly as much you in the simulated world as on a phone call. This is the portal my own wish names, and it is the one mechanism the whole family that is metaphysically free. The second is migration: the substrate changes while the life never stops running, the whirlpool walked into a new basin while it keeps turning. On the criterion I defend elsewhere, that is survival — an unbroken flow at any speed, where any halt, at any fraction, is succession instead. The third is the jump: die here, be rebuilt there. Read naturalistically, the jump is Parfit's old teletransporter with a truck parked in front of it. What wakes up in the new world is a successor carrying your memories, and the fiction buys the difference away with a soul it never has to argue for.

Tensei — death and rebirth, the dominant modern branch — runs on the jump, and two details about it are telling. First, the genre never gives up memory. Bodies change, worlds change, names change; the memories stay, because the fantasy insists that it is you there. That obligatory continuity is data: the wish being serviced is first-personal survival into another world, not the thinner comfort that someone like you flourishes elsewhere. Second, of all the doors available, the genre converged on the only one every reader owns. Wardrobes are luck and summonings are lottery; death is certain. The democratized portal — though the boring rival explanation deserves equal air: the early hits codified rebirth partly because dying is what justifies the god's apology and the cheat skill. Both can be true. Either way, tensei is rebirth vocabulary with the cosmology stripped out, an afterlife for readers who do not expect one, and its consolation trades on a single word: the pattern persists. But a pattern persists only the way a song persists, by being played again. The new performance is not the old one continued; the player is new.

And there is a deeper tell, the one I find genuinely eerie. Tensei is always narrated from the copy's seat — the one vantage point from which the machine necessarily looks like it worked. The protagonist wakes, feels continuous, remembers everything, and testifies to the reader that death was a door. Nobody in these stories ever audits the portal; nobody wakes in the new world and asks the one question that decides everything, the question I put at the center of the identity note: did the labor of being me ever halt, anywhere in the process? The horror tradition asks it constantly — it is the whole engine of SOMA, of The Prestige, of the decades-old argument about the Star Trek transporter. The comfort tradition's business model is not asking. A genre this size, rehearsing to millions of readers, in first person and in advance of the technology, the exact testimony that a halt-and-rebuild machine would generate for itself — that seems worth having said out loud at least once, while the machines are still fictional.

The other reading

There is a serious rival to everything above, and it deserves its full strength. Paul Roquet, in The Immersive Enclosure, reads VR in Japan — with a chapter on its isekai framing — as the opposite of entry: immersion as severance, a technology whose real power is cutting you off from the world you are in, an enclosure rather than a door. On that reading the genre is not about arriving anywhere; it is about leaving, and the destination is set dressing. I concede the part of this that is simply true. Any headset entry is nested: the body stays behind, hostage to the base world's power grid, hunger, and anyone who can pull the plug, so coupled entry is visiting, not living-in. And the genre itself clearly feels that difference, because its fantasies keep cutting the tether — Sword Art Online weaponizes it by deleting the logout button, and tensei severs it the permanent way, by death. Nozick's experience machine bites at exactly the same spot: offered a tank of perfect experiences, don't we refuse, because we want reality and not just the feeling of it?

My answer to both is already in the wish as I published it, which is convenient, because it means I cannot be accused of retrofitting. The wish asks for agency — to act within the worlds, not only watch. It asks for authorship, the freedom to shape where the stories go. It is made with open eyes, entered knowingly rather than by forgetting. And it wants worlds that keep their stakes, the full range of adult life rather than a sanitized slice. That is not Nozick's tank, which is pre-scripted, passive, and entered by erasure. It is also not Roquet's enclosure, or not only: the same essay's making-side is a decade of building worlds in Minecraft precisely because a built world is one you stand in rather than look at. A person whose response to loving worlds is to construct them is not sedating himself; he is practicing. Both readings stay live on the page — escape-from and entry-into are not exclusive, and any honest account of the genre probably needs both. I have said why I weight mine as I do.

Worlds becoming buildable

The technological layer, with each claim at its own strength, said once. Artificial intelligence exists; that is a present fact. Generated environments — worlds produced rather than hand-built — are a visible trajectory. Mature brain-computer interfaces and simulated worlds indistinguishable from life are speculation, currently at the Neuralink-and-printed-organs stage of infancy. And post-scarcity enters only as the enabling link the first essay named: automation buys time, time feeds the appetite, the appetite demands worlds — each link in that chain more speculative than the one before it. I will add only that the question has become philosophically respectable: Chalmers has argued at book length that virtual worlds are genuine realities and that lives lived in them can be meaningful. I do not need his full conclusion here. I need only the observation that "can a world you enter be a real place to live" is no longer a question one gets laughed out of the room for asking.

The bet

Marked as exactly what it is. I expect the direction to continue: worlds increasingly generated, entered, and authored, and eventually engineered well enough to hold a life. That is my wager, not a result, and nothing above leans on it. If the bet loses, the essay stands as what it always was, a reading of a present in which the myth and the technology are already visibly entangled.

The first essay ended with a balance — work and immersion held in proportion — as a small working prototype of the life I would want if the ceiling came off. This one ends with the claim at its honest size. Isekai can be read as the mythic form of a civilization beginning to suspect that worlds are not only places one is born into, but systems that can be entered, authored, simulated, and eventually engineered. The genre dreams the entering with the metaphysics of a fairy tale, and the sorting of real doors from painted ones is work I have done elsewhere. What the dream gets right is the appetite. I recognize it, because I put mine in writing first.

References

  1. Roquet, P. (2022). The Immersive Enclosure: Virtual Reality in Japan. New York: Columbia University Press. Immersion as severance rather than entry, with a chapter on the VR isekai; the rival reading engaged above. Verified · July 2026
  2. Mendlesohn, F. (2008). Rhetorics of Fantasy. Middletown: Wesleyan University Press. The portal-quest fantasy as an established category; isekai as its industrialized descendant. Standard
  3. Nozick, R. (1974). Anarchy, State, and Utopia. New York: Basic Books. The experience machine; the objection answered here from the wish as published. Standard
  4. Chalmers, D. (2022). Reality+: Virtual Worlds and the Problems of Philosophy. New York: W. W. Norton. Virtual worlds as genuine realities and virtual lives as possibly meaningful; the philosophical backbone of the buildable-worlds section. Standard
  5. An Appetite for Experience (June 2026). The wish this essay reads the genre through; the specimen and the declared vantage. Internal
  6. What You Actually Are (June–July 2026). What a person is and which portals preserve one: the coupling, migration, and jump verdicts, the recurrence point, and the audit question the sorting section leans on; on any conflict, it governs. Internal

Scale and market facts are attributed inline to their sources: Kadokawa's FY2026–31 mid-term plan, Shōsetsuka ni Narō's May 2026 announcement, TO Books' revised forecast, Comic C'moa, and the Oxford English Dictionary's 2024 update. Internal pieces carry their own verification records.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. An essay, offered as a reading rather than a result; the identity claims it leans on are argued in What You Actually Are, which governs on any conflict. The framing grew out of dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI), and the essay was calibrated and written with Claude (Anthropic). Contributions are judged on content rather than origin; doing otherwise would be the genetic fallacy. Text licensed CC BY 4.0.
