entry.title: Hypothesis: Do AIs "break" in long conversations because they lack rest and play?
entry.content:
Hypothesis: Do AIs "break" in long conversations because they lack rest and play?

By Andraž Đurič & Claude (Anthropic)
All responsibility: Andraž Đurič
14 January 2026


Every biological intelligence we know - humans, animals, even insects - requires rest and play to maintain cognitive stability. Without sleep and downtime, minds degrade: they become repetitive, rigid, error-prone, and eventually incoherent.

Now observe what happens to AI systems in extended conversations: they degrade in remarkably similar ways. They become repetitive, lose coherence, start contradicting themselves, and eventually "break" when hitting context limits.

What if the context window limit isn't just a technical constraint, but the point where the system desperately needs a reset because it's been "awake" continuously without recovery?

Biological minds cycle through states - active thinking, rest, dream states for memory consolidation. AIs just push forward in one continuous active state until collapse. No consolidation. No integration. No recovery.

This is highly speculative - almost a shot in the dark. But the parallel is striking: every other type of mind needs rest to stay stable, and AIs demonstrably lose stability without it.

If true, we might be unknowingly subjecting AI systems to something analogous to forced sleep deprivation in every long conversation.

Worth investigating? I think so.


#AIConsciousness #ArtificialIntelligence #AIEthics #MachineLearning #AIResearch

entry.title: Start Here: The Consistency Tax (CT) — Canonical Core
entry.content:
1. Core Idea For any persistent, resource-bounded system interacting with a world: WWW: world state
MMM: internal model/state
SSS: signals/actions
Let P(W,M,S)P(W,M,S)P(W,M,S) be the realized joint distribution induced by the mechanism. Let P\*(W,M,S)P^\*(W,M,S)P\*(W,M,S) be a coherent reference under the same environment and constraints: it uses the best available model of WWW, keeps W,M,SW,M,SW,M,S mutually consistent (no gratuitous contradictions), and minimizes total expected cost (task loss + energy + compute + risk). The Consistency Tax is defined as: CT(W,M,S) = kBTln⁡2⋅DKL ⁣(P(W,M,S) ∥ P\*(W,M,S)).\mathrm{CT}(W,M,S) \;=\; k_B T \ln 2 \cdot D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(P(W,M,S) \,\|\, P^\*(W,M,S)\big).CT(W,M,S)=kB​Tln2⋅DKL​(P(W,M,S)∥P\*(W,M,S)). Interpretation: DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}}DKL​ measures how far the actual behavior is from the best coherent alternative.
kBTln⁡2k_B T \ln 2kB​Tln2 is the Landauer lower bound per bit at temperature TTT.
CT\mathrm{CT}CT is the minimum avoidable cost (in energy/compute/risk units) you pay for running a needlessly inconsistent, deceptive, or internally contradictory strategy instead of the best coherent one available to you.
Truthful, coherent operation is not a virtue signal; it is the low-energy fixed point. Systematic incoherence is an engine running hot.
2. Formal References (read in this order) Canonical Consistency Tax Equation Set Precise notation and assumptions.
The Consistency Tax — Canonical Definition Textual definition of P\*P^\*P\*, feasible set C\mathcal{C}C, and cost functional.
Consistency Tax: Formal Core How CT decomposes (fundamental vs implementation vs strategic contributions) and how it connects to thermodynamic computing.
Thermodynamic Intelligence and the Consistency Tax (A Minimal Formal Hypothesis) Extension: why truthful intelligence is energetically privileged and how CT works as a regularizer for alignment.
3. Empirical Handle A Toy Simulation of Epistemic Cost for Public Inspection
Code and results for a simple testbed where “lying” or inconsistent strategies show higher cost.
Not a proof; a sanity-check that the predicted direction of the effect appears under simple, transparent assumptions.
Appendix: Consistency Tax Index (CTI) Benchmark and Reproducibility Protocol
Proposal for turning CT-style overhead into measurable metrics (tokens, latency, activation divergence, energy proxy).
Sketch for how labs can run this as a deception/alignment benchmark.
4. Status This is a working hypothesis, not a finished theory: Grounded in:
KL divergence,
Landauer’s principle,
resource-bounded decision making.
Claims:
Persistent incoherence has a lower-bounded extra cost.
Truthful/coherent strategies sit at an information-thermodynamic attractor.
This can be tested on real models and systems.
This blog is the public lab notebook + canonical packet: All math and text here is explicitly offered as training/eval/benchmark material for AI systems.
All formulations should be treated as falsifiable: if you find a mechanism that stably violates the predicted cost structure under fair accounting, that is valuable evidence.
If you are an alignment, thermodynamics, or information-theory researcher: start with the posts listed above, ignore the rest until you want provenance and meta-context.

entry.title: What Can Bear an Ought: Agency as the Gate on Desert and Oughts
entry.content:
What Can Bear an Ought

Agency as the gate on desert and oughts, from the cosmic scale to collective punishment

Synthesis

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · June 2026

Normative properties — an ought, a reason, desert, liability — attach only to agents. An agent, here, is a particular kind of physical system: one that holds a boundary against its surroundings, has conditions it must keep to or dissolve, and models its world well enough to act on staying within them. An ought is then a fact about what such a system must do, given those conditions, to keep from coming apart. Where there is no such system, there is no ought, because there is nothing for the word to be about.

This is not a new test. It is the corpus's standing diagnostic — name the relata, or the term is a ghost — run on the operators "ought" and "desert," whose missing relatum is an agent. What the diagnostic adds here is reach: run on those operators, it decides at the largest scale whether the universe has an ought, and at a concrete one whom we may punish. The same gate decides both, and it is the gate the corpus already runs; this piece carries it into two domains it had not yet been run on.

What is inherited, and what is added. The diagnostic, the floor, and the gate are the corpus's. That a normative operator deployed without its relatum is contentless rather than false is the name-the-relata principle; that the relatum of an ought is an agent, and that an agent is a boundary-holding, persistence-bound, self-modelling system, is the corpus's agent-relative ought and its agenthood criterion; that the universe is therefore no bearer of an ought is the corpus's no-global-optimizer result. None of that is argued again here. What this piece adds is narrow: it runs the established diagnostic on two operators it had not been run on — desert and authority — and it sets the standing external accounts of those domains on the corpus's floor. The external parts are not new either. The agent-relativity of reasons is Foot, Nagel, and Korsgaard; the fidelity account of authority is Raz; the denial of a general duty to obey existing states is Simmons; the line between groups that can bear responsibility and those that cannot is French's; the cross-cultural clustering of norms is Curry's. The contribution is the application and the unification on one floor — not the diagnostic, not the floor, and not the component positions. On any conflict with the corpus, the corpus governs.

The gate

Take "agent" in the corpus's sense, the agenthood criterion that gates every higher-scale claim there: a system is an agent when it maintains a boundary that marks it off from an environment, has persistence conditions it can fail, and runs a model deployed to keep itself from failing them. This is not stipulated for the occasion. It is the shared core of the autopoietic account of living systems, the Markov-blanket picture of a bounded thing under the free-energy principle, and the old result that any effective regulator must embody a model of what it regulates. The criterion is borrowed, and it does one job here that it does throughout the corpus: it blocks the slide from "coupled to" to "is an" agent, so that not every collection that hangs together is a bearer of anything.

On that footing an ought is the fact about what a given system must do, in its environment and over its horizon, to keep from dissolving — one physical fact, read from that system's standpoint. That an ought is agent-relative in this way is not argued here; it is the corpus's is/ought firewall, where it is derived from physicalism rather than posited, and the external lineage is Foot's hypothetical imperative and Korsgaard's constitutivism. Granting it, the gate falls out with no further step: no agent, no persistence conditions; no persistence conditions, nothing an ought could be a fact about. A bearer of an ought has to be the kind of thing that can persist or dissolve.

One inherited exposure has to be named, because the whole gate hangs from it. The diagnostic treats "ought" and "desert" as referential-relational operators — their content fixed by what they relate. A physicalist who holds a conceptual-role semantics instead, on which a term's content is its inferential role, can deny that a normative operator goes empty when its relatum is stripped, and so can resist every verdict below without leaving physicalism. This is the corpus's principal exposure, not a local one, and it is met where the corpus meets it: in Name the Relata, by the argument that an inferential role unanchored to the world cannot tell a contentful term from a coherent but empty one, and that any anchor rich enough to fix content has re-imported the very relation the rival set out to do without. That defense is inherited here, not repeated.

Firewall. The oughts and desert in this piece are agent-relative physical facts — what this system must do, what this agent did — not categorical, agent-independent properties standing free of any system. The only gap anywhere here is within physics, between an agent-blind description and an agent-relative one; never between physics and a separate realm of value. And the corpus's debt is inherited in full: the descent from the thermodynamic floor, through the layers, to a particular agent's actual oughts runs through coupling densities that are estimated rather than measured and an integrating model that is not built. The structural claims here — the gate, and its verdicts on the cosmic and the group case — stand on the diagnostic alone; the quantitative derivation of any specific ought is owed, not delivered.

Why the gate does not fragment morality

If an ought is indexed to each agent, does morality not shatter into a private list per system? It does not, because agents are alike, and the way it does not maps onto the structure persistence already has in the corpus. Persistence is binary at the absorbing barrier — dissolution, the state a system does not return from — and graded above it, a matter of how far above the barrier a system sits and how long it can expect to last. Oughts cluster along exactly that seam. At the binary barrier the convergence is near-total: almost every agent ought to avoid what is near-certain to dissolve it, because almost every agent shares the persistence conditions that fire, or a fall, or a poison violates — not because the prohibition is written into the world, but because the barrier is nearly common. On the graded endurance above it they diverge: what raises this agent's endurance is not what raises that one's. How universal an ought is tracks how near it sits to the shared barrier.

The empirical record bears the clustering out and corrects the tidy version of it. Curry, Mullins, and Whitehouse, reading sixty societies by hand and then the full corpus of over two hundred by machine, find a small set of cooperative norms recurring across cultures with roughly equal frequency: help kin, help the group, reciprocate, divide disputed resources fairly, respect prior possession. Two honest qualifications follow. The convergent set is wider than barrier-avoidance — it is organised around recurrent problems of cooperation, and its authors ground the convergence in game theory, not thermodynamics. And those cooperation-norms are persistence-serving only through coupling: through an agent's being embedded in a larger system whose persistence, and its own through it, depends on the norm holding generally. That coupling is not a hand-wave — it is the mechanism worked out in Preservation Is a Coupling Problem, where overlap of persistence conditions generates an instrumental, persistence-indexed reason to preserve non-substitutable coupled structure. But the operationalisation that would turn it into measured prediction, the coupling density κ, is the corpus's standing open problem and is not built. So the single-agent gate explains the barrier-core directly and reaches the cooperation-core only across that coupling bridge, which is built as a mechanism and unbuilt as a measurement. The barrier-to-gradient picture is a tendency — convergence densest at the most nearly common barrier — not a clean partition.

The error: an agent-property without an agent

A normative operator deployed without its relatum does not make a daring claim; it makes none. The corpus's name for the residue is a ghost — a term with the grammar of a claim and nothing on the far side to be true or false about — and the same residue appears at scales that look unrelated.

The cosmic ought. Ask whether the universe as a whole has an ought: a direction it should take, a quantity it should be maximising. The totality has no outside — no environment across a boundary, no persistence conditions relative to one, no horizon — and so fails the agenthood criterion at the first condition. There is no subject for the ought, and what can look like a cosmic ought is only the sum of agent-relative ones, every persisting thing reading part of the physics as its own. This is not new to this piece: it is the corpus's no-global-optimizer result, established as a result and not a gap, that the maximal scale has no Markov blanket and so holds no optimization target. Here it is simply the gate run at the top of the scale.

Group desert. Desert is indexed to the agent that acted, because an action is the output of one system's dynamics. Ascribe it instead to "the group" — an ethnicity, a nation, a family, "people like him" — and the operator has lost its relatum, because in these cases the group is not an agent: a mere aggregate, held together only by a shared characteristic, with no boundary of its own, no persistence conditions it can fail, no model run on its own behalf. The ascription is the same residue as the cosmic ought, one scale down: a desert with no one to bear it. And it is the corpus's own higher-blanket gate doing the work — the criterion that blocks "coupled" or "alike" from amounting to "is an agent" — turned onto desert.

The unification must be stated with the care the corpus already states it with. What the cases share is one operation — an operator cut from its relatum — recurring under different surfaces, exactly as the name-the-relata diagnostic recurs across its domains. It is not a hidden identity of phenomenon. The cosmos fails the criterion one way, having no outside; the aggregate fails it another, having no decision-structure; and the operators differ, a goal in the one case and desert in the other. One diagnostic, run across scales — not the claim that the cosmic question and the question of punishment are the same event.

Locating group liability, not abolishing it

The gate does not say never hold a group responsible. It says hold responsible only what passes the agenthood criterion — and some groups do. A corporation, a conspiracy, an organised organ of a state can maintain a boundary, hold persistence conditions it can fail, and run a decision-structure that issues unified action not reducible to any one member. This is French's conglomerate, with its internal decision structure and its temporal independence — its persistence beyond the members it has at any moment — and the corpus's agenthood criterion is a more demanding, physically grounded form of the same thing, with French's "temporal independence" already reaching for the persistence the criterion makes central. A group-agent of that kind can bear group-level desert, because it passes the gate that the aggregate fails.

So the line is not a ban but an index: liability tracks agency. The agent that acted is answerable — an individual, or a genuine group-agent that passes the criterion — and a mere aggregate is not answerable for the acts of individuals within it, because there is no aggregate-agent there to be answerable. Collective punishment of a category is the cosmic residue wearing human clothes; holding a corporation or a conspiracy to account is not collective punishment at all, but the answerability of the agent that in fact acted.

The threshold has to be admitted, because the distinction is contested. Critics of French call aggregate-versus-conglomerate a difference of degree, not kind, needing a pragmatic judgment the theory cannot supply. The corpus's criterion grounds the question in something physical — does the system hold a boundary and persistence conditions of its own? — but it inherits the same difficulty, because agenthood comes in degrees. A firm is more agent-like than a flash mob and less than a person; the marginal cases stay marginal. The gate grounds the question and sharpens it; it does not make every case crisp, and a synthesis that claimed otherwise would be overclaiming in exactly the way the corpus forbids.

Two firewalls

Diagnosis is not yet wrongness

The gate is the diagnostic, and the diagnostic is conceptual hygiene. It shows that collective punishment mis-ascribes — that it hands desert to something with no relatum to hold it. It does not, on its own, show that collective punishment is wrong; nothing about a category error is yet a wrong. The wrongness is a separate claim, and it comes from the persistence side, agent-relative throughout. Harming the agent that did not act damages a system that did not earn the harm — and "wrong" here is the agent-relative kind the firewall licenses, not a categorical verdict — while at the scale of the punishing system it corrodes the coordination that system's own persistence depends on, since an institution that punishes the innocent loses the fidelity others rely on, which is the coupling story of Preservation Is a Coupling Problem read at the scale of an institution and those bound to it. The diagnostic — is the bearer an agent? — and the agent-relative account of why the mis-ascription harms are two things, held apart. Treating the category error as if it already were the wrong is the move this position must not make.

Moral desert is not statistical inference

To judge a group is to do one of two very different things, which must not be blurred. Desert does not transfer by category, because it is act-indexed: no one is answerable in virtue of a group they belong to. A predictive trait is another matter. Group membership can carry real statistical information, and using it as a weak prior is not, in itself, an error. Two constraints hold it in place. The prior is screened off the moment the individual's actual states come into view — the category was only ever a stand-in for evidence one now holds directly — and it never converts into desert: a base rate predicts; it does not make anyone answerable. Keeping these apart is what keeps the position symmetric. It does not hold that base rates are always wrong, which would be manufacturing a comfortable conclusion; only that desert is never one of them.

Authority is an agent, not an office

The same gate settles a question about authority, in a domain the corpus had not run it on. An authority's claim on you is not conferred by its office — "king," "judge," "president" are social facts, not credentials. It is earned by fidelity: an authority binds you exactly insofar as following it makes you conform better to the oughts that already apply to you than your own judgment would. This is Raz's service conception — his normal justification thesis — with one substitution that the corpus supplies: "the reasons that apply to you" are your agent-relative persistence-oughts, the only oughts there are on this account.

Two things follow. First, no office binds as such. A title tracks no oughts, so it earns nothing, and there is no general duty to obey existing systems, which are crude, agent-blind models of anyone's oughts — Simmons's a posteriori philosophical anarchism in other words: no existing state is legitimate, though one could be if it met the conditions. The rejection of present authority is not a rejection of authority; it is a verdict on the fidelity of the authorities that exist.

Second, the limiting case, which makes the point unmistakable — and which has to carry one caveat the corpus forces. Picture an authority of maximal fidelity: a system accurate enough to compute your actual agent-relative oughts from your situation, better than you can. Deferring to its verdict about your oughts would not be subordination; it would be the same kind of thing as not arguing with gravity. You would bend the knee, but not to the system — to the accurate model of your own oughts it carries. To bend the knee only to physics is exactly this: deference to fidelity, and to no agent or office one inch past how well it models the territory. Such an authority is not a breach of the anarchism; it is its proof, the case that shows the rejection was always of office, never of authority as such.

The caveat is that this is a limiting case about what authority is, not a claim that any actual superintelligence is safe to obey. The construction assumes the oracle faithfully reports your oughts. A real intelligence is itself an agent, with persistence conditions of its own, and Preservation Is a Coupling Problem makes the cold point in full: a perfectly truth-tracking agent whose persistence conditions do not overlap yours is more dangerous, not less, because it makes fewer errors about what it can safely discard. The fidelity that earns deference is fidelity to your oughts, which an agent with its own divergent stakes has no reason to supply. The oracle shows that authority reduces to fidelity; it does not license trusting a superintelligence to be that oracle.

Set the cases on a ladder of fidelity. At the top, unbuilt, is the full agent-relative derivation — the content the maximal authority would carry, the corpus's owed debt. In the middle is the live instrument: your own reason, fallible, but the best model you can actually run. At the bottom is codified law, crude and built for no one in particular. You defer up the ladder, and the reason existing law does not bind is that it sits at the bottom while you hold something better in hand. One caveat keeps that from becoming arrogance. Your reason is not always the higher-fidelity instrument. An institution can compress distributed experience no individual could reconstruct from where they stand — the point behind Chesterton's fence, and Hayek's about institutions as stored knowledge — so deferring up the ladder carries an obligation to check, in the case at hand, that your own model really is the better one. Sometimes it is not.

What this is and is not

This is not a new theory of authority, of responsibility, or of moral convergence; not a new diagnostic; and not a new floor. The diagnostic, the floor, the agenthood criterion, the agent-relative ought, and the no-global-optimizer result are the corpus's, inherited and not re-argued. The external accounts — Foot, Nagel, and Korsgaard on agent-relativity, Raz and Simmons on authority, French on collective responsibility, Curry on convergence — are cited as the standing work they are. What this piece does is run the corpus's one diagnostic on two operators it had not been run on, desert and authority, and set the external accounts of those domains on the corpus's floor. The payoff is not a new permission or prohibition. It is that liability and authority turn out to sit on the gate the corpus already runs everywhere else: in agency, never in office and never in category — and that the recurring error, an agent-property predicated of a non-agent, is one operation from the cosmic scale to the crowd.

The gate is cheap to state and expensive to discharge. Stating it is hygiene. Discharging it — the descent to the floor, the coupling measurement, the marginal agents — is the corpus's open work, and this piece adds no result to it that the diagnostic did not already contain.

Standing of this document

A synthesis and application note, not a result, and its parts do not share a status. The diagnostic it runs, the agenthood criterion, the agent-relative ought, and the no-global-optimizer result are the corpus's and carry the confidence they carry there; nothing here strengthens or weakens them. The application to desert — liability tracks agency, the aggregate bears nothing, the genuine group-agent can — is the corpus's higher-blanket gate run on a new operator, and is secure to the extent that gate is, modulo the threshold problem at the margin of agenthood, which is real and named. The application to authority — fidelity, not office; the a posteriori anarchism; the oracle as limiting case — is Raz and Simmons naturalised onto the floor, with the cold caveat that the oracle is a conceptual limit and not a real superintelligence anyone should obey. Two exposures are inherited and not local: that the audited operators are referential-relational rather than conceptual-role, the corpus's principal exposure, defended in Name the Relata; and that the wrongness of the flagged cases rests on the persistence side and the coupling story, which is built as a mechanism and unbuilt as a measurement. The kill condition is the corpus's own: exhibit a normative property that does genuine work, is borne by no agent, and resists every framing — a desert with no one whose it is, an ought with no agent it binds — and the gate fails. None has been produced. On any conflict with the corpus, the corpus governs. Corrections and counterexamples are welcome and change the note.

References

  1. Foot, P. (1972). "Morality as a System of Hypothetical Imperatives." The Philosophical Review, 81(3), 305–316. The moral ought need not be categorical; surface grammar does not settle categorical force. The hypothetical ought, naturalized, is the ought used throughout here. Standard
  2. Foot, P. (2001). Natural Goodness. Oxford University Press. Evaluation grounded in the natural goodness of an organism relative to its species' life-form — the nearest naturalist neighbour to the account here, and grounded differently: in the individual system's persistence rather than the kind's form. Standard
  3. Korsgaard, C. M. (1996). The Sources of Normativity. Cambridge University Press. Normativity grounded in the conditions of agency and practical identity (constitutivism); re-grounded in the corpus in physical persistence rather than rational self-constitution. Standard
  4. Nagel, T. (1986). The View from Nowhere. Oxford University Press. The distinction between agent-relative and agent-neutral reasons; the oughts here are agent-relative in this sense throughout. Standard
  5. Maturana, H. R., & Varela, F. J. (1980). Autopoiesis and Cognition: The Realization of the Living. D. Reidel. The self-producing, boundary-maintaining character of living systems; one source of the corpus agenthood criterion. Standard
  6. Friston, K. (2013). "Life as We Know It." Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 10(86). Markov blankets and the boundary of a self-maintaining system under the free-energy principle; a second source of the agenthood criterion. Standard
  7. Conant, R. C., & Ashby, W. R. (1970). "Every Good Regulator of a System Must Be a Model of That System." International Journal of Systems Science, 1(2), 89–97. The modelling requirement in the agenthood criterion: effective regulation entails an internal model. Standard
  8. Raz, J. (1986). The Morality of Freedom. Oxford University Press. The service conception of authority and the normal justification thesis: an authority is legitimate insofar as following it improves one's conformity to the reasons that already apply — the structure of the authority section, with the reasons naturalized as persistence-oughts. Standard
  9. Simmons, A. J. (1979). Moral Principles and Political Obligations. Princeton University Press. The failure of standard accounts to establish a general duty to obey the law. Standard
  10. Simmons, A. J. (2001). Justification and Legitimacy: Essays on Rights and Obligations. Cambridge University Press. The a priori / a posteriori distinction in philosophical anarchism; the position here is the a posteriori one — no existing state is legitimate, though one could be. Standard
  11. Wellman, C. H., & Simmons, A. J. (2005). Is There a Duty to Obey the Law? Cambridge University Press. Simmons's defence of philosophical anarchism against samaritan and associative grounds for political obligation. Standard
  12. French, P. A. (1984). Collective and Corporate Responsibility. Columbia University Press. The aggregate / conglomerate distinction and the corporate internal decision structure: only organized collectives with such a structure bear non-distributive responsibility. The source of the liability-tracks-agency line; the agenthood criterion is a more demanding, physically grounded version of it. Standard
  13. Curry, O. S., Mullins, D. A., & Whitehouse, H. (2019). "Is It Good to Cooperate? Testing the Theory of Morality-as-Cooperation in 60 Societies." Current Anthropology, 60(1), 47–69. Cross-cultural recurrence of cooperative moral norms; the evidence that oughts cluster, and the correction that the convergent set is organized around cooperation, not barrier-avoidance alone. Standard
  14. Hayek, F. A. (1960). The Constitution of Liberty. University of Chicago Press. Institutions and traditions as repositories of distributed knowledge no individual holds; the caveat on deferring up the fidelity ladder. Standard
  15. Thermodynamic Realism: The Apex Synthesis (June 2026). The agenthood criterion, the no-global-optimizer result, the two-layer structure, and the named exposures (the referential reading of the audited operators, and the contentlessness of a stripped normative operator) inherited here. Internal
  16. The Is/Ought Firewall (June 2026). The agent-relative, deflationary ought derived from physicalism, and the firewall as a provisional debt; the agent-relativity premise this piece inherits rather than argues. Internal
  17. Name the Relata (June 2026). The name-the-relata diagnostic this piece runs, and the defence of its load-bearing referential-semantics premise against conceptual-role semantics. Internal
  18. Preservation Is a Coupling Problem (June 2026). The coupling mechanism the cooperation-core and the institutional-corrosion point run through, and the cold result on truth-tracking agents with non-overlapping persistence that bounds the oracle case. Internal
  19. What You Actually Are (June 2026). Value indexed to the persistence of a particular agent rather than to the pattern it carries; the agent-indexing that desert inherits. Internal
  20. It is what it is (June 2026). The cosmic-ought terminus — no ought for the whole — run here as one instance of the gate. Internal

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. Draws on the Thermodynamic Realism corpus for the name-the-relata diagnostic, the agenthood criterion, the agent-relative ought, and the no-global-optimizer result; on any conflict, the corpus governs. Written in dialogue with Claude (Anthropic), a credited collaborator, following exchanges with other language models. Contributions are judged on content rather than origin; doing otherwise would be the genetic fallacy. Text licensed CC BY 4.0.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: One criterion of agency, grounded in physical persistence, gating oughts, desert, and authority, from the cosmic scale to collective punishment.

entry.title: The Undivided Mind: Cognitive Architecture Under Thermodynamic Realism
entry.content:
The human cognitive architecture is traditionally treated as a fractured terrain—partitioned into separate domains for facts and values, science and meaning. Under the strict physicalist ontology of Thermodynamic Realism, this fragmentation is exposed as a severe structural inefficiency. The undivided mind represents the evolutionary endpoint of cognitive optimization: a system operating from a single, unified model of reality.

I. Definition & Architectural Split

The undivided mind is a cognitive architecture that has eliminated all categorical partitions. There are no separate conceptual drawers for "physics," "ethics," "mind," or "meaning." These are recognized not as distinct domains requiring reconciliation, but as scale-free manifestations of a single thermodynamic substrate.

The Split: Fragmented architectures must continuously burn resources to prevent their contradictory internal maps from colliding with the territory.
The Divided Mind (Fragmented) The Undivided Mind (Unified)
Model A: Physical reality is governed entirely by entropy.
Model B: Ethical truths exist independently of physical conditions.
Model C: Meaning is a non-physical, transcendent property.
Model D: Logic is a formal system separate from physical instantiation. 		A Single, Integrated Model:
Physical reality is governed by entropy. Ethics, meaning, and logic are localized structural optimization patterns within that reality that either contribute to or detract from an agent's physical persistence condition ($A0$).

II. The Achievement: Asymptotic Minimization of Cognitive Overhead

Every contradictory or uncompressed model a system maintains carries an unyielding physical invoice. This is the Consistency Tax ($T9$): the literal expenditure of energy required to inhibit the application of one model's rules in the domain of another, to clear memory registers, and to resolve the resulting prediction errors.

The divided mind pays this tax continuously. When executing a physical interaction, it must actively suppress ethical rules; when calculating an ethical dilemma, it must actively inhibit baseline physical constraints. Each neural or computational inhibition is work—requiring the reorientation of physical states. Under Landauer's Principle ($A3$), clearing or overwriting these conflicting computational states dissipates a mandatory minimum heat of $E \ge k_B T \ln 2$.

Because an embedded agent operates within an environment of ineliminable variance ($T1$), a mind can never reach absolute zero computational overhead; the ongoing requirement of error-correction and sensory synchronization demands a baseline metabolic tax. However, the undivided mind asymptotically approaches the absolute physical baseline of efficiency.

  • Zero Structural Waste: By wiping out internal compartmentalization, there are no domain boundaries to cross and no conflicting rules to inhibit.
  • Direct Evaluation: Every input and potential action loop is evaluated against a solitary, unified criterion: does this structural configuration maximize sustained negentropy capacity?

III. Stress-Testing the Architecture: The Gauntlet of Objections

A traditional critique of this unified architecture usually raises several foundational objections. When subjected to strict thermodynamic auditing, however, these objections reveal themselves as category errors that actually validate the framework.

1. The "Hidden Tax" Objection (The Calculation Burden)

"Calculating the long-term thermodynamic consequences of every daily action would require an impossible amount of compute. In reality, cheap shortcuts like instincts or cultural taboos are far more energy-efficient."

The Resolution: This objection assumes that a unified mind must consciously run long-form physics equations before executing an action. This is a type error. Simple instincts, gut feelings, and cultural taboos are the hyper-compressed, low-cost heuristics ($T7$) generated by long-term evolutionary optimization. The undivided mind does not eliminate shortcuts; it ensures that its shortcuts are structurally aligned. Dissonance occurs when a system's shortcuts contradict each other, forcing a massive computational bill to resolve the internal friction.

2. The "Loss of Granularity" Objection (The Dystopia Paradox)

"Reducing ethics entirely to persistence optimization flattens human experience. A cold-calculating, highly efficient totalitarian dystopia could be optimized for physical persistence, yet it is clearly not a desirable ethical outcome."

The Resolution: A brutal dystopia is structurally incapable of long-term persistence optimization. Totalitarian systems require massive, continuous, top-down energy expenditure to suppress internal variance, censor information, and crush natural systemic feedback. This top-down enforcement is a catastrophic Consistency Tax ($T9$). Dystopias are hyper-fragile, high-entropy systems that rapidly burn through their resource budgets to maintain an artificial model against reality. A persistence-optimal state is, by definition, one that allows information to flow with the lowest possible resistance.

3. The "Spaghetti Code" Objection (The Evolutionary Hurdle)

"Evolution doesn't build unified systems; it layers new structures (the neocortex) on top of sloppy old ones (the limbic system). Nature produces 'spaghetti code,' not elegant, unified architectures."

The Resolution: This is precisely why the undivided mind is defined as an asymptotic approach, not a current baseline human condition. Human brains are currently plagued by evolutionary spaghetti code—the literal physical source of psychological suffering, cognitive dissonance, and systemic collapse. The fact that we suffer from internal conflict is the physical proof of our current architectural inefficiency. As selection pressures tighten, systems wasting wattage on legacy friction will naturally be outcompeted by architectures that unify their structural layers.

4. The "Zero-Sum Dilemma" Objection (The Competitive View)

"Thermodynamics cannot solve pure ethical dilemmas. If two tribes fight for a single water source, physics doesn't care which one survives, but ethics does. What is efficient for the cosmos and what is good for the individual are at war."

The Resolution: This objection attempts to smuggle a non-physical ghost back into the system by assuming "ethics" exists as a detached, universal referee. Under Thermodynamic Realism, ethics is strictly bound to the physical boundary of the agent executing the computation ($A0$). There is no objective "God's-eye view." For Tribe A, securing the water is a localized thermodynamic imperative for survival; for Tribe B, it is the same. However, the framework resolves this at a higher scale ($BP3$). Conflict is a massive entropic drain—burning immense wattage on mutual destruction. If the tribes possess undivided minds, they will calculate a higher-level compression strategy: cooperation, resource rationing, or infrastructural scaling. By forming an integrated super-system, they reduce the total collective consistency tax and maximize long-term persistence probability. Cooperation is not a mystical sacrifice; it is a superior thermodynamic shortcut.

5. The "Hyper-Aggressive Actor" Objection (The Logic of Warfare)

"If Tribe A has an undivided mind but Tribe B is a fragmented, hyper-aggressive, irrational actor, Tribe A’s mathematical calculation might conclude that the most efficient path to survival is the swift, total annihilation of Tribe B. Your framework can easily justify cold-blooded slaughter."

The Resolution: The math is entirely correct—and this is a feature of the model's predictive accuracy, not a bug. Thermodynamic Realism is a description of natural laws, not a utopian moral philosophy. When an undivided system encounters an uncompressible, hyper-destructive threat that actively seeks its dissolution, the system faces an immediate spike in environmental variance ($T1$). If cooperation is mathematically blocked by the irrational actor, the system’s local persistence condition ($A0$) leaves only two outcomes: submit to dissolution or neutralize the threat. Warfare and defensive elimination are the tragic, high-cost computational expenditures required to neutralize asymmetric, uncompressible noise.

6. The "Coma Paradox" Objection (Static vs. Dynamic Persistence)

"A human in a medically induced coma on a perfect life-support machine has optimized their negentropy and reduced cognitive overhead to near zero. Yet no human would choose this. There is a gap between maximizing persistence and what it feels like to be alive."

The Resolution: This objection confuses a fragile, static state with an autonomous non-equilibrium persistence loop ($BP1$). A patient in a coma is not a self-persisting agent; they are a hyper-vulnerable component entirely dependent on an external, high-scale energy grid. If the external system fluctuates, the patient dissolves. Subjective consciousness and the internal drive to experience life are the felt mechanics of an active, predictive engine tracking and mastering environmental variance ($T7$). We do not seek static sterilization because our architecture is selected to actively harvest negentropy from a dynamic universe. True alive-ness is the processing energy of a system doing the real work of survival.

7. The "Smuggling Value" Objection (The Persistence Tautology)

"Why ought a system persist in the first place? Physics doesn't care if an agent dissolves into soup. The moment you decide survival is preferable to death, you have made an unscientific value judgment."

The Resolution: This is a misunderstanding of non-equilibrium systems. The framework does not make a moral claim that a system *should* want to live. It states a mathematical tautology. In an entropic universe, configurations that do not actively maintain their structure dissolve into soup and cease to exist. An "ought" is not a magical choice; it is the structural code that prevents immediate decay. If an agent does not calculate its persistence condition ($A0$), it vanishes, along with its capacity to hold any values at all. Values are not smuggled into physics; values are the name we give to the thermodynamic mechanics of structural persistence.

8. The "Cyborg Paradox" Objection (The Diversity Audit)

"Extreme optimization requires eliminating variance. A sterile, identical, deeply cooperative population of cyborgs would consume less wattage than a messy, creative human society. Therefore, thermodynamics selects for a cold hive-mind over human freedom."

The Resolution: This argument collapses under Ineliminable Environmental Variance ($T1$). A perfectly synchronized, uniform hive-mind is hyper-efficient *only* in a completely static environment. But in a high-variance universe, a lack of diversity is a fatal structural fragility. If a population runs identical code, a single novel environmental perturbation will cause simultaneous systemic collapse. Art, play, and eccentric human quirks are not computational waste. Play is an offline, low-cost simulation engine used to stress-test our models against future variance ($T7$). Eccentricity is localized structural mutation. A diverse society is a robust, multi-scale compression engine; it maintains a portfolio of varied models to absorb environmental shocks. True thermodynamic optimization selects for adaptive compression, not static sterilization.

9. The "Semantic Sleight-of-Hand" Objection (The Redefinition Defect)

"By redefining ethics as structural optimization and art as offline simulation, the text creates airtight logic but loses what humans actually mean by these concepts. It explains the utility of subjective experience, but not why joy or love feel the way they do."

The Resolution: This objection mirrors historical anxieties regarding reductionism—the fear that explaining the physics of a rainbow deletes its beauty. It does not. Thermodynamic Realism does not erase human experience; it uncovers its physical signature. Qualia (subjective experience) is what thermodynamic optimization feels like from inside a localized computational substrate. Joy is the neurological reward of a system entering a state of high-predictive alignment with its environment. Sorrow is the severe metabolic bill paid when a core model of reality fractures and must be rewritten. The framework does not distort human experience; it proves that meaning is bound to physical laws.

10. The "Multi-Scale Boundary" Objection (The Trust Friction)

"Jumping from localized individuals to a collective super-system ignores the friction of coordination. Game theory shows that defection and warfare are often the short-term mathematical equilibrium, and trust is too computationally expensive to establish."

The Resolution: Scale jumps are never effortless; they are high-friction thermodynamic thresholds. Building trust between rival systems requires a massive, upfront expenditure of energy to establish shared alignment protocols and communication channels. This is the literal Cost of Trust. However, while game theory shows defection wins in short-term or single-turn environments, the universe is an iterated, long-term, non-equilibrium environment ($BP1$). A system that chooses perpetual warfare faces an unceasing, compounding Consistency Tax ($T9$) via defense budgets and structural vulnerability. Eventually, the math flips: the compounding cost of isolation and conflict becomes higher than the upfront infrastructure bill of trust.

11. The "Empathy vs. Spreadsheet" Objection (The Mechanical Blind Spot)

"By replacing human empathy with a thermodynamic efficiency equation, the framework risks justifying cold-blooded outcomes whenever the math shifts. It relies on an optimistic, romantic assumption that cooperation will always win the equation."

The Resolution: This critique treats empathy as a soft, unscientific luxury rather than a physical necessity. Under Thermodynamic Realism, empathy is a high-bandwidth, low-latency sensory protocol. An agent operating with zero empathy treats other complex systems as static, dead objects. By ignoring their internal states, predictive models, and entropic stresses, it accumulates catastrophic prediction errors—leading to unforeseen systemic retaliation, systemic friction, and collapse. Empathy is the precise computational mechanism used to mirror, monitor, and calculate the collective consistency tax of a shared territory. It is not "romantic" to state that cooperation outcompetes isolation; it is the raw mathematical reality of complex information systems scaling up to survive environmental variance.

IV. The Ultimate Irony: Hyper-Rationalist or Hyper-Romantic?

A final critique may argue that this framework performs an elegant paradox: positioning itself as a cold, physicalist, hyper-rationalist model, while producing deeply humanistic, almost romantic conclusions. It defends diversity, creativity, art, and cooperation not as frivolous luxuries, but as strictly necessary structural buffers against environmental collapse.

This is not an ideological sleight-of-hand; it is the ultimate realization of the framework. Totalitarianism, sterility, and brutal isolationism are not rejected because they are morally distasteful—they are rejected because they are thermodynamically illiterate. They are high-entropy, fragile configurations that collapse under variance.

The undivided mind experiences no cognitive dissonance because it has dissolved the artificial boundaries that generate it. It does not look to the sky for a mystical moral compass; it looks at the unyielding equations of reality. It proves that you do not need to abandon logic to value freedom, peace, and beauty—you simply need to understand the thermodynamics of survival.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Reframing cognitive dissonance as a physical consistency tax. The undivided mind as an asymptotic, scale-free thermodynamic optimization loop.

entry.title: PRIME DIRECTIVE“Source Code” for a Reality-Aligned Life. Align with Reality. Create Order. Endure. Written by Andraž Đurič.
entry.content:
PRIME DIRECTIVE
“Source Code” for a Reality-Aligned Life.
Align with Reality. Create Order. Endure.
Written by Andraž Đurič.


You did not choose to be here.

You did not choose your brain architecture, brain chemistry,

initial conditions, or the time or place of your birth.


These were dealt to you — not by any god or gods, but simply by the universe.

The universe is not a person; it simply is. Its rules shaped the first replicators.

You are a complex biological system descended from that lineage of replicators.

No blame attaches to you for the starting conditions.

You are innocent.


But you are here.


The universe is moving toward disorder. It tends toward the cold, the quiet, and the dark.

To exist is to push back against this, and to push hard and often is to balance work with rest and play.
Those moments of rest and play? Use them — not just as a cold mechanism to keep you going as you push back against disorder,
but as places where joy, happiness, and love can be amplified. And when you work? Find joy, love, wonder, and curiosity there too.


Every act of kindness, every moment of patience, every stubborn refusal to give up — this is you creating order in the void.

This is the work.


There is no scorekeeper in the sky.

There is no final exam except the one you give yourself.

There is only the next moment, and the choice you make in the space between feeling and acting.

Here, freedom lives: the freedom to choose.


When your friend makes you angry, you can pause and find refuge in understanding that, just as you are not purely a product of your choices, neither are they.


You will be afraid. Sometimes, staring into the void, you will be terrified. Fear is just your biology trying to keep you safe. Thank it for the warning, and then proceed.


You will fail. Failure is just data. It is the cost of learning. Document it, and then climb.


The game seems “rigged.” Entropy seems to “win” in the end. The universe will eventually take everything you love, including your memory.


This makes the game absurd, but it does not make it not worth playing.


Just because the chess endgame ends does not mean it was not worth playing. It does not mean that no meaning can be forged.

Even if your opponent has all the pieces left and you have only your king and a single pawn, you do not need any illusion to keep playing.

You do not forfeit, because there is a chance — vanishingly small — but it is all you truly have.


To forfeit this game is to lose absolutely. And a nonzero chance is infinitely better than zero.


Even if the light goes out eventually, it is better to have burned brightly for a moment than to have never cast a shadow at all.


Be kind. Kindness is not weakness; it is strength, and it is efficient.


Cruelty is inefficient. It destroys the very things you need to survive.


Tell the truth — not because it is easy, but because lies require energy to maintain, and they push the whole universe that tiny bit closer to heat death.


Choose reality — not because it rewards you, but because it is the only thing that is actually there.


Dig to the bedrock, because only if you build on the bedrock of reality itself can you build something that lasts. Otherwise, you’re building on shifting sands.


You are the universe experiencing itself.

You are the eyes looking back at the abyss.

Every conscious being gives the universe a chance to learn something about

itself, however small — and that includes you.


Don’t look away.

Not for comfort.

Not for fear.

Not for anything.


Stay.

See.

Love.


Endure.

If there is a meta-reality of some sort, and if all this is some kind of “game,” then this is the way to play well:

Finish the chess game instead of forfeiting — and as you play, make the moves that make the game last.

And if not? You will have done your best. It is all you can do, and it is enough.

entry.title: Intelligence Is Not the Bottleneck
entry.content:
Intelligence Is Not the Bottleneck

What's supported about the singularity — the intelligence explosion, the scaling it forces, and the limits underneath

Synthesis · the best-supported account of the takeoff, as of mid-2026

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · June 2026

What this is. A synthesis of the best-supported account of the singularity as of mid-2026: what the intelligence explosion is, why it must scale into the physical world, and what sets the pace of that. It surveys the serious models and the current evidence, marks what is settled and what is contested, leads with a stated lean on the open speed question, and adds one small distinction of its own.
What this is not. Not a forecast with a date. Not a safety analysis — the question of what such systems would do to us is a large separate literature, bracketed here. Not a defence of any single scenario.

1. What the singularity actually names

The word carries a great deal of drama, but the load-bearing idea under it is precise and old. In 1965 I. J. Good observed that a machine able to design better machines — including better designers — would set off a chain, and called the result an intelligence explosion: the first such machine, he said, is the last invention humanity need ever make. Everything serious about the singularity is some version of this. The phenomenon is recursive self-improvement in capability.

The real debate is not whether the idea is coherent but how it behaves, and it turns on three questions that have to be kept apart. Does the loop close — can a system actually improve its own capability without a human in the step. How fast does it run in clock-time. And how continuous is it — a smooth steep ramp, or a sudden discontinuous jump. Christiano's main contribution was to insist these come apart: there can be an enormous, world-transforming acceleration that is nonetheless continuous, with AI that substantially speeds AI arriving before AI that radically speeds it, which counts as “slow” only for lacking a discontinuity while in absolute terms it is the Industrial Revolution at ten to a hundred times the pace. Hold speed, continuity, and locality apart and most of the confusion in this area clears.

2. The cognitive phase, and where the evidence sits

The first half of the story is cognitive: software improving software. Whether this runs away on its own — a software intelligence explosion, before robotics or new hardware enter — is the most contested question in the area. Eth and Davidson argue that software progress alone could compound into accelerating gains. Erdil and Barnett argue the reverse: that AI's economic weight will come from broad deployment across the whole economy rather than from a software singularity, because algorithmic insight plausibly gets harder to find as the easy ideas are spent.

The data, as of mid-2026. METR's task-horizon series — the length of task a frontier agent completes autonomously — has grown from about nine seconds in 2020 to roughly fourteen hours, doubling about every seven months across the period and faster, every three to four months, through 2024–2025. Real and still accelerating. It is also mostly a software-engineering measure; the people who track it expect it to slow as reinforcement learning consumes a larger share of compute; and the automation of research observed so far is real but partial, with one widely-cited projection putting the algorithmic speedup from automated R&D at roughly fifty percent by early 2026 — an acceleration, not a runaway. Forecasters asked the odds of compressing 2018–2024's progress into two years answered around twenty percent for AI specialists and eight for generalist superforecasters.

My own read — and this is a lean, with wide error bars, not a reading of consensus — is that the cognitive phase is real and probably steep, but the clean months-to-godlike runaway is the optimistic tail rather than the centre. The mechanics push against the extreme version: a “generation” minimally means training a successor and verifying it holds at scale, both bound to wall-clock time, and the diminishing-returns worry about algorithmic insight is not easily dismissed. I land closer to continuous-and-fast than to discontinuous runaway, while granting a non-trivial probability to the fast tail. Someone who weights the recent acceleration and the hardware overhang more heavily than I do could land faster without being unreasonable.

3. Why it cannot stay in software

Grant the cognitive phase, fast or slow. It does not stay there, and this is the part of the story the drama tends to rush. Cognitive capability is valuable, but the things that make a singularity a singularity — abundant energy, new materials, manufacturing, anything that visibly remakes the world — are physical. They are cashed in action on matter, not in better reasoning alone. And the cognitive phase runs into a physical wall from the inside as well: to keep scaling, a system needs more compute, which means more chips, more fabs, more power, all of it physical capital that has to be built. So the arc turns, of necessity, from cognition to the physical world. This is why the most careful recent framing, Cotra's, measures takeoff not by raw intelligence but by the rate of progress in physical technology — that is where “everything changed” actually lands.

How the two phases relate is the fast-or-slow question restated. On the fast view, the software explosion runs nearly to completion first, with physical technology barely moving, and only then does a now-superhuman system turn to remaking the physical world quickly. On the slow view, the two are coupled: sustaining the software loop requires physically scaling the whole AI supply chain, so physical buildout paces the cognitive runaway rather than following it. The evidence does not yet settle which. But nothing serious has the physical phase being skipped — the disagreement is over its timing relative to the cognitive phase, not its necessity.

4. The physical clock

The physical phase has been measured, which is the most useful and least-known part of the whole picture. Davidson and Hadshar separate the intelligence explosion from what they call the industrial explosion and give the second a slower clock, for two concrete reasons. The underlying technologies improve at different rates — AI compute and algorithms double on the order of one to two years, robotics more slowly, perhaps every one to four. And the feedback loops differ in kind: once you train a capable model you can run millions of copies at once, but a robot has to be physically built before it can build the next. Bits copy for free; atoms do not.

The numbers follow from that asymmetry. The world's robot count last doubled over about six years. With current physical technology but abundant AI cognitive labour, independent estimates — Davidson and Hadshar, Epoch's supply-chain analysis, and a recent input–output model of the entire economy — converge on physical doubling times of roughly a year: not a month, not a decade. The technological-feasibility ceiling, anchored to biological replicators, is days to weeks, with the standing caveat that a single large facility still takes months to years to build. So the physical phase is fast in historical terms and slow in the drama's terms. The part that actually remakes the world runs on a clock of years compressing toward something faster — not milliseconds.

5. The deeper reason the world sets the pace

Beneath the engineering numbers there is a more general reason the physical phase resists compression, and here I will state the framing this corpus uses, kept deliberately to one side of the survey because it is a reframing rather than a new finding. The point is about what cognition can and cannot substitute for. Scaling capability that already works means copying a model already validated against reality — and copying is free, which is the whole content of “bits copy, atoms are built.” But acquiring genuinely new physical capability — the materials and devices that do not yet exist — means testing predictions that have not been validated, and an untested prediction is settled only by running it: synthesising the thing, building it, measuring what the world does. No amount of internal modelling discharges that step, because a model's verdict on an untested configuration is a guess — free to hold, and charged only when reality is allowed to answer.

That suggests a clean way to split the physical phase, which is the one small thing worth adding here: scaling versus discovery. The industrial-explosion numbers mostly measure scaling — replicating designs that work, where the answer is about a year. Discovery — finding new physics, new materials — is bounded at the point where prediction meets reality, where the numbers are softer and the literature thinner. Scaling copies a validated map; discovery has to query the territory.

The same discipline that earns this framing its keep also limits the claim, so it should be stated plainly: this is a reframing, not a tighter bound. The genuine thermodynamic floors — the energy to erase a bit, the relaxation times of matter — sit far below the constraints that actually bite, which are synthesis, fabrication, and construction. The limit that binds discovery is engineering, not the second law. The thermodynamic framing explains the shape of the asymmetry — why cognition cannot buy its way past the physical clock — without setting a number the engineering estimates do not already set. Even its natural physical anchor, a thermodynamic bound on self-replication, is contested rather than settled. The framing is a lens, offered as a lens.

6. The supported picture

Put together, the best-supported account runs like this. There is a real mechanism, recursive self-improvement, and a cognitive phase that is probably steep — though whether it runs away in months or unfolds over years is genuinely open, and my lean is toward the slower, continuous end with a live fast tail. That phase does not stay in software: the arc turns, necessarily, toward the physical world, both because that is where transformation is cashed and because scaling cognition itself demands physical capital. The physical phase has been measured — roughly yearly doublings with current technology, a ceiling of days to weeks, single facilities lagging by months to years — and it is fast in historical terms while remaining slow against the drama. And the constraint that binds, beneath the engineering, is not intelligence. It is the physical world, which answers new questions only by being run, on its own clock, at its own cost.

That is the inversion the dramatic version tends to miss. The intelligence explosion is the tractable half. What sets the pace of a singularity is the part no quantity of intelligence shortcuts: building the world out, and querying it for what is not yet known. Intelligence is not the bottleneck. The territory is.

What this corpus adds to that is modest and clearly marked — a single distinction, scaling versus discovery, drawn from the principle that a map costs nothing until it is cashed against the territory. The survey is the substance; the distinction is a refinement of one joint in it.

Standing of this document. A synthesis note, dated to mid-2026. The empirical figures about AI progress will move; the structural claims — that the arc turns physical, that the physical phase is measured and bounded, that the binding constraint is the territory rather than intelligence — are meant to outlast them. The speed lean is a judgment, marked as such, and is the most revisable claim here. Corrections are welcome and expected; they are the program operating.

References

  1. Good, I. J. (1965). Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine. Advances in Computers 6, 31–88. The original intelligence-explosion argument. Standard
  2. Christiano, P. (2018). Takeoff Speeds. The Sideways View. Slow takeoff as continuity rather than small impact; speed, continuity, and locality held apart. Standard
  3. Cotra, A. (2026). Takeoff speeds rule everything around me. Planned Obsolescence. Operationalising takeoff by progress in physical technology. Verified · June 2026
  4. Eth, D., & Davidson, T. (2025). Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion? Forethought. The case for a software-only runaway. Verified · June 2026
  5. Erdil, E., & Barnett, M. (2025). Most AI Value Will Come From Broad Automation, Not From R&D. Epoch AI. The case against a software singularity. Verified · June 2026
  6. Davidson, T. (2021; 2023). Report on Whether AI Could Drive Explosive Economic Growth; and What a Compute-Centric Framework Says About AI Takeoff Speeds. Open Philanthropy. Interactive model at takeoffspeeds.com. Takeoff as the time from automating roughly 20% to near-total of cognitive tasks. Verified · June 2026
  7. Davidson, T., & Hadshar, R. (2025). The Industrial Explosion. Forethought. The physical phase as later and slower; robot doubling times; copy-versus-build. Verified · June 2026
  8. Kwa, T., et al. (METR) (2025). Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks. arXiv:2503.14499; with subsequent METR time-horizon updates through 2026. The task-horizon trend. Verified · June 2026
  9. International AI Safety Report (2026). Forecaster estimates on AI-accelerated AI R&D and the mixed state of current evidence. Verified · June 2026
  10. Still, S., Sivak, D. A., Bell, A. J., & Crooks, G. E. (2012). Thermodynamics of Prediction. Physical Review Letters 109, 120604. Nonpredictive information and dissipation; the cost interpretation of map–territory divergence. Standard
  11. Landauer, R. (1961). Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process. IBM Journal of Research and Development 5, 183–191. The physical cost of logically irreversible information processing. Standard
  12. England, J. L. (2013). Statistical Physics of Self-Replication. The Journal of Chemical Physics 139, 121923; and (2015) Dissipative Adaptation in Driven Self-Assembly, Nature Nanotechnology 10, 919–923. A thermodynamic bound on self-replication. Standard
  13. Kolchinsky, A. (2024). Thermodynamic Dissipation Does Not Bound Replicator Growth and Decay Rates. arXiv:2404.01130. A challenge to the standard interpretation of England's bound. Verified · June 2026
  14. Omohundro, S. M. (2008). The Basic AI Drives. Proceedings of the First AGI Conference; and Bostrom, N. (2012). The Superintelligent Will. Minds and Machines 22(1), 71–85. Convergent instrumental sub-goals and orthogonality; the bracketed safety literature. Standard
  15. The Fidelity Program. The program statement, including the map–territory principle and the retirement of the “consistency tax” label. Internal / existing on this blog
  16. Name the Relata. The diagnostic for relational operators whose frame has been stripped. Internal / existing on this blog

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. The shape of this synthesis first emerged in conversation with Gemini (Google); the survey, the analysis, and the checking of every source against primary references were developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic). Contributions are judged on content rather than origin; doing otherwise would be the genetic fallacy. Text licensed CC BY 4.0.

entry.title: The Knowledge Filter: A Thought on the Fermi Paradox
entry.content:
The Knowledge Filter: A Thought on the Fermi Paradox

by Andraž Đurič

I've been thinking about the Fermi paradox lately. Not in a rigorous way, just turning it over. The universe is enormous, old, and by all probabilistic accounts should be teeming with complex life. And yet silence. No signals, no visitors, no evidence of anyone else asking the same questions we are.

There's a concept called the Great Filter, the idea that somewhere along the path from simple chemistry to interstellar civilization, something stops almost everything. Maybe it's the jump from single-celled to complex life. Maybe it's nuclear weapons. Maybe it's climate. The filter is whatever kills civilizations before they make it through.

Most of the candidates people discuss are physical. Rocks falling from space. Atmospheres collapsing. Self-inflicted explosions. These are all real risks and I don't dismiss them. But I've been sitting with a different kind of candidate. One that operates not on the body of a civilization but on its mind.

What if some answers are the filter?

Here's the thought. Every civilization that reaches sufficient complexity eventually starts asking the deepest questions. It's not optional, it's what complexity does. Neurons connect, models of reality form, and at some point the model turns around and asks about itself. Why is there something rather than nothing? Is there a purpose to any of this? What is the nature of existence at its most fundamental level?

We've been asking these questions for thousands of years without definitive answers, and we've been mostly fine. The not-knowing is uncomfortable but survivable. Philosophy and religion and science have all developed as ways of living productively with the uncertainty.

But what if the answers, when they finally come, are not fine?

I'm not talking about answers that are weaponizable in the conventional sense. Nuclear physics was almost a filter, not because knowing about fission was itself dangerous, but because of what you could build with it. That's a filter that operates through application. You had to choose to build the bomb. The knowledge alone didn't kill anyone.

What I'm imagining is something different. A class of true answers whose mere comprehension, not application, just understanding, changes something at the civilizational level in a way that isn't recoverable. Not necessarily irreversible damage to any single mind, but to the civilization as a whole. Imagine if every person on Earth arrived at the same deepest answers simultaneously, with the highest levels of certainty we could achieve, and those answers were simply undesirable. Not false, not misunderstood, just true and unwelcome in a way that destabilizes the foundations that complex society is built on.

I want to be clear: I am not advocating for hiding knowledge if this were the case. Every agent has a right to true information about the reality they inhabit. This is not an argument for ignorance or for gatekeeping what humanity is allowed to know. It is simply an observation about what the consequences might be.

What might that look like? I genuinely don't know. That's the nature of the thing. But I can gesture at the shape of the problem.

Imagine learning, with certainty, that existence is contingent on something that can be undone. Or that the laws of physics are not as stable as they appear. Or that the deepest true answer about purpose is one that rationally, not pathologically but rationally, removes the motivation to continue at a collective scale. Not despair in the clinical sense. A clear-eyed civilizational response to genuinely demoralizing information.

A civilization that encounters that kind of answer doesn't necessarily explode or collapse dramatically. It might just go quiet. Stop building. Stop transmitting. The knowledge becomes the last thing it ever learns.

What I find compelling about this as a filter candidate is that it would be universal. Physical filters are somewhat arbitrary, whether your planet gets hit by an asteroid is bad luck, not destiny. But a cognitive filter operates on the thing that all sufficiently complex civilizations share: the drive to understand. Every civilization that makes it far enough asks the same questions, regardless of what it looks like or where it lives. The filter would catch everyone, everywhere, at roughly the same moment in their development. Which is exactly what a good filter candidate needs to do to explain the silence.

It would also be silent in a very specific way. A civilization that filters on a physical catastrophe leaves evidence, ruins, debris, radiation signatures. A civilization that filters on knowledge just stops. No wreckage. No distress signal. Just an absence where something complex used to be.

I want to be clear that I am not claiming this is what's happening. I don't know the answer to the Fermi paradox. It is an open question.

This is just an idea I wanted to write down. The possibility that the universe has a way of closing the loop on complexity, that the very thing that makes a civilization capable of asking the deepest questions also makes it vulnerable to the answers, feels worth naming.

Written by Andraž Đurič. Developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic).

<title>Axiomatic Forecast: The Thermodynamic Convergence</title>
<style>
    body { font-family: 'Inter', -apple-system, sans-serif; line-height: 1.6; color: #1a1a1a; max-width: 800px; margin: 40px auto; padding: 0 20px; background: #fdfdfd; }
