Why survival across open-ended time requires correction, exploration, and transformation

Position note · open-ended persistence, adaptation, correction, suffering, and valence

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · July 2026

Abstract

This essay develops one consequence of the persistence account used across the Epistemic Forge corpus.

Persistence is easily pictured as resistance to change: hold the present configuration fixed, suppress disturbance, minimize risk, and remain. That picture works only across a sufficiently short horizon and inside an environment treated as stable. Once the horizon is left open and environmental perturbation is admitted, the criterion changes. A system with a fixed repertoire cannot answer conditions outside that repertoire. If consequential variation continues to arrive, incapacity to sense, learn, revise, or transform raises the probability of dissolution.

Adaptive capacity is therefore not imported as a value separate from persistence. Under changing and incompletely known conditions, it is one of the things persistence physically requires. Correction, exploration, knowledge acquisition, redundancy, variation, and transformation become parts of the persistence machinery.

This has a further implication for suffering. Open-ended persistence requires sensitivity to adverse conditions, but sensitivity, nociception, negative signalling, conscious unpleasantness, and severe suffering are not one phenomenon. Evolution joined many of them in biological agents; that does not establish that every possible adaptive architecture must do the same. A civilization that abolishes all adverse information would become fragile. A civilization that preserves precise warning and motivation while reducing severe suffering is a different possibility.

The normative standing is not neutral. Once a bounded valuer is fixed, persistence is good for it in the constitutive sense that only through persistence does any continuing domain of good exist for that valuer; what sustains that persistence is therefore what the agent ought to do relative to its actual organization, environment, and horizon. The stronger content-reduction — that every value reduces, in what it is about, to persistence — remains a live bet. The working hypothesis stated here leaves one exposure open: conscious valence may be an additional physically realized welfare dimension not exhausted by persistence.

1. The mistaken picture

Persistence is often imagined as staying the same.

A system survives, on this picture, by resisting disturbance. The safer system is the more insulated one. The ideal organism is protected from injury, the ideal institution suppresses instability, the ideal civilization removes risk, and the ideal person can be frozen at a tolerable state and held there.

The image has an obvious source. Across a short interval, change is often what destroys. Heat denatures tissue. Impact breaks bone. Mutation disrupts function. Political upheaval can collapse infrastructure. A sealed container may outlast an exposed one. A dormant organism may survive conditions that kill an active one.

None of this is false.

The error is to carry a local strategy across an open horizon and call the result persistence itself.

Resistance to change is one possible response to one class of disturbance. It is not a general solution to continued existence under conditions that themselves change.

A system can remain unchanged only while the conditions required by that unchanged organization remain available.

The dependency may be hidden outside the chosen boundary. A frozen person appears static, but the refrigeration system is active. The refrigeration system depends on energy, maintenance, replacement parts, knowledge, institutions, and protection from larger disturbances. Freezing the person does not abolish the work of persistence. It relocates that work into the surrounding system.

Extend the horizon. Machinery fails. Political orders change. Resources move. Pathogens evolve. Ecologies reorganize. Planets undergo catastrophe. Stars leave the conditions under which their planets formed. The frozen body has no response of its own to any of this. Its apparent durability is borrowed from whatever dynamic system continues to sense, repair, relocate, and protect it.

The point is not that every static object must quickly disappear. Some structures are extraordinarily durable. The point is conditional and probabilistic:

Under environmental perturbation and an open-ended horizon, systems incapable of adaptation acquire a higher probability of dissolution.

This is the central claim of the essay. Everything else develops its consequences and marks its limits.

2. What an open-ended horizon means

An open-ended horizon is not a claim that time is literally infinite, that the universe certainly lasts forever, or that an agent should calculate an infinite sum.

It is a scope decision.

No arbitrary terminal date is privileged in advance. The system is evaluated not merely by whether it survives the next minute, year, lifetime, or century, but by whether its present organization preserves the possibility of continuation across whatever future conditions become physically available.

This matters because strategies reverse their ranking when the horizon changes.

Storing all resources rather than spending any may protect a system through a brief shortage and destroy it when the stored resources decay. Avoiding every dangerous experiment may reduce immediate accidents and leave a civilization unable to understand a threat already approaching. Centralizing every function may improve short-term coordination and create one point at which failure becomes terminal. Suppressing disagreement may stabilize a regime this decade while blinding it to errors that accumulate across the next.

The open horizon does not make immediate survival irrelevant. There is no long term for a system that crosses an absorbing boundary now. It does, however, forbid treating local risk reduction as automatically identical to global persistence.

At minimum, persistence across an open horizon depends on the relation among:

  • the system's present organization;
  • the range of environmental conditions it can tolerate;
  • the disturbances it can detect;
  • the responses it can generate;
  • the speed with which detection can alter response;
  • the resources available for repair and transformation;
  • and the unknown conditions not yet represented in its model.

A fixed design can be excellent inside a fixed range. The problem begins when the range moves.

3. Static durability and adaptive persistence

Two concepts should therefore be separated.

Static durability

Static durability is the capacity to retain a present configuration despite disturbance.

Hardness, insulation, dormancy, redundancy of identical parts, suppression of variation, and resistance to deformation can all contribute to it. It is real and often indispensable.

Adaptive persistence

Adaptive persistence is the capacity to preserve the relevant continuity of an organized system by changing its states, components, models, strategies, or location as conditions require.

An organism persists adaptively. It replaces matter, repairs tissue, regulates temperature, reallocates energy, learns regularities, modifies behaviour, and sometimes reconstructs damaged organization. Its continuity is not identity of state. It is continuity of organized work through state change.

The same structure appears at larger scales. A language persists while its vocabulary changes. A scientific tradition persists by replacing theories. An institution can preserve its function by revising procedures. A civilization can preserve its lineage while changing its energy systems, settlements, bodies, and forms of governance.

Persistence across change is not the preservation of every present feature. It is the preservation of the organization or lineage whose continuation is being evaluated, through whatever transformation that continuation requires.

This creates an identity debt. Before claiming that a transformation preserved a system, one must specify what counted as constitutive of that system.

A regime may preserve its name while destroying the population, practices, values, and correction channels that previously made it that regime. A person may remain metabolically alive while losing the psychological organization ordinarily meant by personhood. A civilization may retain biological descendants while ending every institution and memory by which its historical continuity was tracked.

Something persisted in each case. Whether it was the thing originally under evaluation depends on the boundary and criterion of identity.

Adaptive persistence is therefore not permission to redescribe any successor as survival. Transformation must remain continuous with the organized process or lineage whose fate is at issue. The relevant continuity has to be argued, not granted by vocabulary.

4. Why correction follows

A finite agent cannot carry a complete model of the environment through which it must persist.

Its sensors sample. Its memory selects. Its concepts compress. Its predictions are limited by evidence, computation, time, and the possibility that the relevant future state has not yet entered its possibility space.

The agent must act through this incomplete map anyway.

Where the map diverges from the territory, action meets consequence. A prediction fails. A resource disappears. A structure is damaged. A rival behaves differently than expected. A previously stable regularity changes. If the consequence can alter the model or the activity guided by it before dissolution, the system possesses a correction pathway.

Across a stable, narrow environment, a fixed policy may persist without much learning. Across a changing environment, uncorrected divergence accumulates.

A system that cannot be changed by the consequences of its errors is adapted only to the conditions its present model already captures.

This is where persistence and fidelity meet.

Correction is not a decorative intellectual virtue added after survival has been secured. For model-bearing systems under uncertainty, it is part of how survival remains possible when the map is incomplete.

The requirement is architectural, not attitudinal. A civilization may praise criticism while censoring the evidence that would make criticism effective. An organization may collect feedback while rewarding subordinates for hiding failure. A person may declare fallibility while interpreting every counterexample through a self-protective model.

Correction requires a functioning route:

  • a consequential variable must be sensed;
  • the signal must be distinguishable from noise;
  • the divergence must be compared against some standard;
  • the model or policy must be updateable;
  • and the update must reach action before the error becomes irreversible.

A system can fail at every step while still appearing informed.

Persistence does not demand that every signal trigger revision. Overreaction to noise is itself destabilizing. The requirement is not maximum change but calibrated change: enough stability to preserve accumulated structure, enough plasticity to answer conditions the structure did not already encode.

5. Why exploration and knowledge follow

Correction is reactive. It begins when some divergence has already entered the system.

An open horizon also rewards anticipatory contact with what has not yet become an immediate error.

Exploration expands the represented territory. Scientific inquiry reveals threats, resources, mechanisms, and possibilities before ordinary action collides with them. Engineering turns those discoveries into new response capacities. Movement and dispersal expose a lineage to new environments while reducing dependence on one location. Counterfactual modeling allows a system to test possibilities without paying their full physical cost.

Exploration carries danger. Spaceflight can fail. New technologies can create new hazards. Biological experimentation can release damage. Contact with unfamiliar systems can destabilize old ones.

But the comparison is not between risky exploration and riskless stasis.

The comparison is between the known risks introduced by exploration and the accumulating, partly unknown risks of remaining confined to the present model, repertoire, and location.

A civilization that never leaves one planet avoids the risks of leaving and retains every risk correlated with that planet. A civilization that forbids dangerous research avoids some research accidents and remains vulnerable to dangers the forbidden research might have revealed or controlled. A species optimized to one present environment may outperform a more varied population now and be unable to survive when the environment changes.

Experimental work on evolutionary rescue shows the physical shape of the argument in a limited domain: populations declining after environmental deterioration can avoid extinction when adaptive evolution occurs quickly enough. Experimental evolution has also produced bet-hedging in bacteria exposed to fluctuating conditions, where phenotypic variation spreads risk across states the lineage cannot predict in advance.

These results do not establish a universal theorem for civilizations. They establish the mechanism in real systems: variation and adaptive change can trade some local performance for increased persistence under changing conditions.

Knowledge is therefore not merely something a persisting agent happens to enjoy after maintenance is complete.

Under uncertainty, knowledge acquisition modifies the system's reachable futures.

6. Requisite variety, redundancy, and option space

A regulator can answer only disturbances for which it has some differentiating response.

A thermostat that can switch heating on or off regulates a narrow range of thermal variation. It cannot repair a broken furnace, detect carbon monoxide, relocate the building, redesign the power grid, or model the climate. Each new disturbance class requires additional sensing, control, or reorganization somewhere in the coupled system.

Cybernetics captures this through requisite variety: successful regulation requires enough response variety to constrain the variety that matters in the regulated system.

The lesson is often misunderstood as a demand that the regulator contain a detailed copy of everything outside it. That would be impossible for a finite agent. The requirement is indexed to consequential variation and can be met through several strategies:

  • better sensors;
  • a larger response repertoire;
  • learning and recombination;
  • delegation across specialized subsystems;
  • environmental modification;
  • redundancy;
  • distribution across locations;
  • and reduction of disturbances before they reach the protected variables.

This is why diversity can be persistence-serving without becoming sacred in itself. A population containing several response types may survive a disturbance that eliminates a uniform population. Competing models may preserve alternatives when the dominant model is wrong. Redundant institutions may look inefficient until one fails. Cultural experimentation may retain solutions whose relevance is invisible under current conditions.

Not all variation helps. Many mutations are damaging. Many political alternatives are worse. Many speculative theories are false. Variety carries maintenance and coordination costs.

The open-horizon claim is therefore not “more diversity is always better.” It is:

A system that removes every unused alternative because it is locally inefficient may also remove the response required by a future condition it cannot yet predict.

Persistence can require preserving generative capacity: the ability to produce responses not explicitly stored in advance.

Learning, recombination, imagination, play, scientific freedom, and technological flexibility may all contribute to that capacity. Their value is partly that the future need not already be represented at full resolution for the system to answer it.

7. Institutions can persist by becoming unable to persist

The distinction becomes politically important.

An institution can increase local stability by suppressing disagreement, narrowing permitted information, centralizing authority, punishing deviation, and making leadership difficult to replace. These measures may genuinely extend the life of the current ruling structure.

They may also degrade the larger system's ability to detect and answer reality.

Bad news moves upward more slowly. Local failures are hidden. Models become selected for political safety rather than correspondence. Succession becomes dangerous. Policy errors compound because the institution has made correction look like disloyalty.

This produces an apparent paradox only while the relatum remains vague.

The ruling coalition may persist while state capacity falls.

The state may persist while the population is damaged.

The civilization may persist while one regime disappears.

The social lineage may persist by replacing the institution that had begun to treat its own continuation as the whole.

Persistence of a subsystem can conflict with persistence of the system in which it is nested.

That is why “the larger system” is not an adequate phrase. Larger by what boundary? Constituted by which processes? Over which horizon? A cancer cell and an organism are both persisting systems. The cell's success can be the organism's failure. A censorship apparatus and a civilization are both organized processes. The first may preserve itself by impairing the second's model of reality.

Institutional corrigibility is therefore not automatically a universal moral command. It is a persistence-relevant capacity whose necessity depends on the system, environment, and horizon. Under sufficiently changing and complex conditions, however, eliminating independent correction channels raises the risk that consequential divergence will remain hidden until repair is no longer available.

A competent institution needs memory and continuity. It also needs pathways through which reality can defeat the institution's current model without first defeating the institution itself.

8. Name what persists

Every claim in this essay is indexed.

“Persistence is improved” is incomplete until the bearer is named.

At least the following must be specified:

  • Which organized process? A cell, person, family, institution, civilization, biosphere, or lineage?
  • Which boundary? Material, organizational, control, legal, explanatory, or some combination?
  • Which constitutive features? Bare physical continuity, agency, memory, culture, conscious subjects, values, or function?
  • Which environment? What external processes supply resources, threats, and maintenance?
  • Which horizon? Immediate survival, expected duration, or open-ended continuation?
  • Which uncertainty? What possibilities and model failures are represented, and what remains outside the model?
  • Which coupling? Whose persistence depends on whom, with what substitutability?

Without these relata, unlike processes are collapsed into one word. A rock enduring, a cancer expanding, a person remaining alive, a regime retaining control, and a civilization preserving its adaptive lineage are all cases of continuation at some boundary. They are not therefore the same normative object.

Indexing does not remove the good. It locates it.

For a bounded valuer, persistence is good because it maintains the domain in which anything can continue to be good for that valuer.

Once the agent, boundary, environment, and horizon are fixed, the relevant is-facts can yield an ought: trajectories that sustain the agent are what it ought to enact; trajectories that dissolve it are failures relative to that agent. The ought adds no nonphysical property. It names the agent-indexed sustaining relation.

This does not imply a categorical command issued by the universe, nor the first-order policy “maximize your own duration at every cost.” An agent may value another process above its own continuation, and nested agents can possess conflicting persistence conditions. Nor does one selected boundary automatically override the persistence or suffering of every other agent. Those are further indexed conflicts requiring the actual couplings to be modeled.

Firewall. The firewall does not prohibit deriving an ought from an is. It holds the index in place and marks where the integrating model is still unpaid. Persistence is good for the persisting valuer; what specifically advances it can be inferred only after the agent, organization, environment, horizon, uncertainty, and relevant couplings are named.

The demand to name the bearer also prevents one easy rescue of the theory.

When a cruel or rigid system persists, it is tempting to say that it is not “real,” “healthy,” “higher-order,” or “viable” persistence. But unless those adjectives are independently derived, they import the conclusion that persistence alone was supposed to provide.

The cleaner move is to index the case. The tyranny may persist as a regime and damage the population, knowledge network, conscious subjects, and civilizational adaptability on which other persistence trajectories depend. No adjective is needed. The conflict appears once the relata are restored.

9. The comfort mistake

If persistence requires keeping systems away from damaging states, one might infer that the ideal civilization should eliminate every discomfort, frustration, threat, and negative experience.

That inference repeats the stasis error at the level of experience.

A system that suppresses every indication that something is wrong does not thereby remove what is wrong. It removes its access to the difference.

Consider a civilization that defines perfect comfort as the absence of every adverse signal. Pain is suppressed. Fear is suppressed. Prediction error is hidden. Failure produces no frustration. Institutions cannot issue alarms that disturb citizens. Every mismatch is translated into reassurance.

Such a civilization may feel stable while damage accumulates outside awareness.

Open-ended persistence requires sensitivity to what is going wrong.

This sensitivity need not take one form. It may involve automatic protective reflexes, nociception, homeostatic error, cognitive recognition, negative affect, social warning, institutional audit, scientific anomaly, or direct repair before any conscious state becomes intense.

The important distinction is between abolishing damage and abolishing information about damage.

Reducing preventable injury, disease, scarcity, coercion, and trauma removes sources of suffering by changing the territory. Anesthetizing every response while leaving the causal structure untouched changes only the map available to the agent.

A high-comfort civilization can therefore be adaptive if comfort is produced through superior prediction, prevention, repair, and signal design. It becomes fragile when comfort is produced by making adverse states phenomenally or institutionally invisible.

10. Signal is not suffering

The discussion requires a stricter vocabulary.

At least five layers can be distinguished:

  1. Environmental perturbation: a change outside or inside the system.
  2. Damage or threat: a perturbation that moves the system toward loss of organization, capacity, or valued state.
  3. Detection and control signal: a state that indicates the divergence and alters response.
  4. Negative conscious valence: an experience felt as unpleasant or aversive by a conscious subject.
  5. Severe suffering: negative experience of sufficient intensity, duration, inescapability, or organization-disrupting effect.

These layers interact, but they are not identical.

Nociception is the nervous system's detection and processing of noxious stimulation. Pain is a conscious experience. Human pain itself contains distinguishable sensory and affective dimensions: experimental modulation can change unpleasantness without changing the represented sensory intensity to the same degree.

Congenital inability to experience pain shows the protective importance of the system. People lacking ordinary pain sensation can accumulate fractures, burns, tissue damage, and self-injury that pain would normally interrupt.

But this establishes only that removing a major warning and motivational channel from a human body is dangerous. It does not establish that greater pain always improves regulation, that chronic suffering remains useful after its informational role is exhausted, or that every possible agent must implement threat sensitivity through the same phenomenal architecture.

The evidence that no pain is dangerous does not show that maximum pain is optimal.

Severe suffering can itself degrade the capacities a corrective signal is supposed to protect. It can narrow attention, impair deliberation, disrupt memory, damage trust, produce avoidance detached from the original threat, and make future learning less accurate. Even where aversion is useful, intensity and duration remain engineering variables.

Evolution did not design pain from a position of global foresight. It retained mechanisms that were good enough to alter behaviour and reproduction under ancestral constraints. Those mechanisms can be protective, excessive, miscalibrated, or persistent after their immediate function has changed.

A future civilization should not assume that the inherited implementation is the necessary limit.

11. The adaptive aversive budget

A working concept follows.

An adaptive aversive budget is the minimum negative signalling or experience required by a given agent architecture, in a given environment, to detect consequential divergence, prioritize response, learn, and remain capable of correction.

The phrase does not assume that conscious aversion is fundamentally necessary. It marks the quantity to be investigated rather than decided in advance.

For present human beings, some unpleasantness may be functionally difficult to remove without weakening motivation or protection. Hunger, pain, fear, frustration, grief, and social distress each participate in control systems that were not built as detachable modules.

But their current presence does not settle three separate questions:

  • How much negative valence is required for the function?
  • Can the same function be implemented through a different conscious or nonconscious signal?
  • Can earlier prediction and automatic repair prevent the state that would have required the signal?

A technologically mature civilization could reduce the budget from several directions.

It could detect tissue damage before pain becomes severe. It could preserve urgency while removing panic. It could separate informational salience from overwhelming unpleasantness. It could provide reversible challenge rather than uncontrolled trauma. It could design institutions in which failure is visible without making disclosure personally ruinous. It could repair causes rather than repeatedly intensifying warnings.

The optimum would not be one fixed number. It would vary with embodiment, cognitive architecture, environmental volatility, available repair, and the cost of missed signals.

A persisting agent under changing conditions may require enough adverse signalling to register consequential divergence and compel correction, but no greater intensity or duration than the function requires.

This is a research direction, not a completed metric. The important move is to stop treating “suffering” as one indivisible package whose protective functions justify every part of it.

12. Does persistence absorb valence?

The new argument resolves one pressure against persistence and leaves another open.

The normative floor is already fixed. For a bounded valuer, persistence is good because without it there is no continuing domain in which anything can be good, pursued, corrected, suffered, enjoyed, or valued by that agent. Given the agent and its conditions, facts about what sustains or dissolves it yield agent-relative oughts.

What remains open is not whether persistence is good. It is whether persistence exhausts the content of every good.

The new argument weakens the objection that persistence must favor frozen stasis, complete risk avoidance, epistemic closure, or permanent institutional lock-in. Across changing conditions and an open horizon, these strategies can lower the adaptive capacity on which continuation depends.

It also explains why much suffering should be reduced on persistence grounds. Severe suffering commonly damages bodies, cognition, cooperation, trust, exploration, and correction. A civilization that systematically destroys the agents performing its sensing, learning, and maintenance is often reducing its own open-ended persistence.

But “often” is not “necessarily,” and the stronger content-reduction cannot be completed by adding favorable adjectives to persistence.

Consider the remaining question in indexed form.

Suppose two trajectories preserve the same conscious agents for the same duration, with the same adaptive capacity, knowledge, relationships, option space, and probability of continued persistence. In one trajectory, corrective signals are experienced as severe suffering. In the other, the same informational and motivational work occurs with minimal negative valence.

If the trajectories are genuinely equal in every persistence-relevant respect, does the content of persistence alone contain the difference between them?

The intuition behind sentience-centered ethics says no. On that reading, the suffering trajectory is worse for the subjects undergoing it because the negative character of the experience is itself a physically realized fact about their welfare.

That intuition is evidence for a rival or supplementary account, not yet a derivation. The secure normative claim remains that persistence is good for the valuer and grounds its oughts; the unresolved claim is whether valence ultimately bottoms out in that same persistence relation.

The thought experiment may conceal persistence effects not held constant in practice. Conscious valence may be more deeply constitutive of agency, preference, learning, and self-maintenance than the clean separation assumes. A complete physical theory could eventually show that the apparent extra dimension is one aspect of a richer persistence relation.

Or it may show that persistence and valence are distinct higher-level dimensions realized by the same physical system.

Secure claim. Persistence grounds the continuing domain of value for a bounded valuer and the agent-relative oughts that follow from its actual persistence conditions.

Working hypothesis. Conscious valence may be an additional physically realized welfare dimension whose content is not exhausted by persistence.

On this hypothesis, persistence explains why there remains a valuer and a domain of good for it. Valence further describes how a trajectory is experienced by that valuer.

This is not a return to nonphysical value. The experience is a state of a physical conscious subject. Any welfare significance it has is indexed to that subject, not issued by the universe as a categorical command.

Under the working hypothesis, “suffering is bad” must therefore be expanded:

Suffering is negatively valenced for the conscious subject whose state it is; whether that fact reduces entirely to the subject's persistence conditions, and how conflicts across agents are aggregated, remain further problems.

The universe still has no owner and no global ought. The web contains local agents, local welfare, nested persistence conditions, and real conflicts among them.

13. What the argument does and does not establish

The argument establishes a conditional architecture inside an already agent-relative normative account: persistence is good for the bounded valuer, and the facts of what sustains it determine its oughts once the relevant index is fixed.

Where:

  • a bounded system has conditions under which it persists or dissolves;
  • its environment can vary in consequential ways;
  • its model and response repertoire are finite;
  • and no fixed terminal date closes the evaluation in advance;

then incapacity to detect, learn, revise, or transform raises the system's vulnerability to conditions outside its present repertoire.

From this follow several persistence-relevant capacities:

  • correction;
  • exploration;
  • knowledge acquisition;
  • generative variation;
  • redundancy and distribution;
  • preservation of option space;
  • and transformation continuous with the system or lineage under evaluation.

The argument does not establish:

  • that every change is adaptive;
  • that exploration always outweighs caution;
  • that diversity is valuable without cost or limit;
  • that a system should sacrifice present viability for arbitrarily small future possibilities;
  • that every persisting entity is a valuer;
  • that persistence of one agent overrides all others;
  • that conscious suffering is required by every possible adaptive architecture;
  • or that conscious valence has been proven irreducible to persistence.

The status of the suffering claim is therefore exact.

Open-ended persistence requires sensitivity to what is going wrong. Evolution built much of that sensitivity through suffering, but an advanced civilization may be able to preserve the information and motivation while reducing the suffering component dramatically.

Whether every persistence-promoting role of suffering can in principle be replaced remains open.

Whether valence ultimately reduces to a sufficiently complete account of persistence remains open.

The working hypothesis keeps both questions available to correction.

14. Persistence, compressed again

A system exists inside conditions it does not control completely.

Its present organization fits only some range of those conditions.

Its map is incomplete.

Its response repertoire is finite.

Across a short interval, insulation and resistance may be enough.

Across an open horizon, the range can move.

What cannot sense the movement cannot correct for it.

What cannot generate a new response remains confined to the old range.

What suppresses adverse information protects its current model from the evidence that the model has failed.

What eliminates every unused alternative may eliminate the one response a future condition requires.

Persistence therefore changes its appearance.

It is not a thing held motionless.

It is continuity earned through work, correction, exploration, and transformation.

A system that cannot change cannot reliably persist through a changing world.

And for conscious systems, one question remains after continuation has been secured:

Not only whether the valuer remains, but how remaining is for the valuer.

Standing of this essay

This is a position note extending the persistence and correction architecture of the Epistemic Forge corpus. It is not a proof that all enduring systems must become more complex, a universal optimization theorem, or a completed reduction of value.

The strongest claim is conditional: under consequential environmental perturbation, finite response capacity, and an open-ended horizon, systems incapable of adaptation acquire a higher probability of dissolution. Adaptation is not introduced as an independent good in that argument. It is derived as a persistence requirement under those conditions.

The post's principal contribution is to distinguish static durability from adaptive persistence and to draw the consequences for correction, exploration, knowledge, institutional openness, variety, and adverse signalling.

The suffering section makes three claims at different standings.

High confidence: adaptive systems require sensitivity to consequential divergence; abolishing every adverse signal would impair correction.

Supported but implementation-relative: biological pain has protective functions, while its sensory and affective dimensions are partly dissociable and severe suffering can exceed or impair those functions.

Open: whether conscious negative valence is necessary in every possible adaptive agent and whether all valence reduces in content to persistence.

Secure normative claim: persistence grounds the continuing domain of good for a bounded valuer, and agent-relative oughts can be inferred from the physical facts of what sustains or dissolves it once the relevant index is fixed.

Working hypothesis: conscious valence may remain an additional physically realized dimension of welfare whose content is not exhausted by persistence.

The essay should be corrected at the points where those dependency classes are wrong, not protected by treating the open labels as permanent exemptions from resolution.

References

  1. Ashby, W. R. (1956). An Introduction to Cybernetics. Chapman & Hall. — requisite variety and the formal relation between disturbance, regulation, and the range of available responses. Standard
  2. Barandiaran, X. E., Di Paolo, E., & Rohde, M. (2009). "Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-Temporality in Action." Adaptive Behavior, 17(5), 367–386. — agency as a graded organization involving individuation, normativity, and asymmetric regulation. Verified · July 2026
  3. Beaumont, H. J. E., Gallie, J., Kost, C., Ferguson, G. C., & Rainey, P. B. (2009). "Experimental Evolution of Bet Hedging." Nature, 462(7269), 90–93. — experimental evolution of phenotypic risk spreading under continually changing selective conditions. Verified · July 2026
  4. Bell, G., & Gonzalez, A. (2009). "Evolutionary Rescue Can Prevent Extinction Following Environmental Change." Ecology Letters, 12(9), 942–948. — experimental evidence that sufficiently rapid adaptation can reverse decline under environmental deterioration. Verified · July 2026
  5. Conant, R. C., & Ashby, W. R. (1970). "Every Good Regulator of a System Must Be a Model of That System." International Journal of Systems Science, 1(2), 89–97. — the regulator-model result used here only at its scoped control-theoretic level. Standard
  6. Cox, J. J., Reimann, F., Nicholas, A. K., Thornton, G., Roberts, E., Springell, K., et al. (2006). "An SCN9A Channelopathy Causes Congenital Inability to Experience Pain." Nature, 444(7121), 894–898. — loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A and the absence of ordinary pain sensation in humans. Verified · July 2026
  7. Di Paolo, E. A. (2005). "Autopoiesis, Adaptivity, Teleology, Agency." Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 4, 429–452. — adaptivity as regulation relative to viability rather than bare continued self-production. Verified · July 2026
  8. Holling, C. S. (1973). "Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems." Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics, 4, 1–23. — the foundational distinction between narrow stability and persistence across disturbance. Verified · July 2026
  9. Maturana, H. R., & Varela, F. J. (1980). Autopoiesis and Cognition: The Realization of the Living. Reidel. — self-producing organization as background to the distinction between static presence and active maintenance. Standard
  10. Montévil, M., & Mossio, M. (2015). "Biological Organisation as Closure of Constraints." Journal of Theoretical Biology, 372, 179–191. — organization through mutually dependent constraints that contribute to maintaining the system. Verified · July 2026
  11. Popper, K. R. (1963). Conjectures and Refutations. Routledge. — fallibilism and correction through exposure to possible refutation; used here as epistemic lineage, not as a biological derivation. Standard
  12. Rainville, P., Duncan, G. H., Price, D. D., Carrier, B., & Bushnell, M. C. (1997). "Pain Affect Encoded in Human Anterior Cingulate but Not Somatosensory Cortex." Science, 277(5328), 968–971. — experimental modulation of pain unpleasantness supporting a distinction between affective and sensory dimensions. Verified · July 2026
  13. Rainville, P., Carrier, B., Hofbauer, R. K., Bushnell, M. C., & Duncan, G. H. (1999). "Dissociation of Sensory and Affective Dimensions of Pain Using Hypnotic Modulation." Pain, 82(2), 159–171. — further experimental separation of pain intensity and unpleasantness. Verified · July 2026
  14. Zhang, Y., & Haga, N. (2014). "Skeletal Complications in Congenital Insensitivity to Pain with Anhidrosis: A Case Series of 14 Patients and Review of Articles Published in Japanese." Journal of Orthopaedic Science, 19(5), 827–831. — recurrent skeletal injury where ordinary pain protection is absent. Verified · July 2026

Verification key: "Verified · July 2026" means the citation and the specific claim attributed to it were checked during this writing pass. "Standard" means the work is treated as canonical background and was not independently re-checked in full during this pass.

Internal lineage

This position note develops and narrows arguments from the Epistemic Forge corpus, including:

  • The Natural History of Fidelity;
  • Value as Persistence;
  • The Is/Ought Firewall;
  • Where the Is–Ought Question Bottoms Out;
  • What Can Bear an Ought;
  • The Exclusivity Error;
  • What You Actually Are;
  • The Fidelity Program;
  • The Spine and the Web;
  • Preservation Is a Coupling Problem;
  • and the current working hypothesis on persistence and conscious valence.

On conflict, the later apex synthesis and the modules whose questions are directly at issue govern. This note adds one derived claim to that architecture: once the horizon is open and the environment is permitted to change, persistence must be modeled as continuity through correction and transformation rather than as fixed-state preservation.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia.

Developed through the Epistemic Forge corpus and dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI). The argument, scope decisions, and final editorial responsibility remain the author's. Contributions are assessed by their content rather than their origin.

entry.title: The Dissolution of the Is-Ought Distinction - An Agent-Relative Semantics Grounded in Persistence
entry.content:
The Dissolution of the Is-Ought Distinction

An Agent-Relative Semantics Grounded in Persistence

Abstract The is-ought distinction, as articulated by Hume (1739), asserts that normative conclusions cannot be derived from descriptive premises by valid deductive inference. This paper argues that the apparent gap between fact and value is a semantic artefact rather than an ontological feature of reality. The argument proceeds in three steps. First, the term "ought" functions as a regulatory operator whose semantic content presupposes an agent with persistence-conditions; deployed outside this presupposition, "ought" claims are type-errored rather than false (§2). Second, any agent capable of formulating "ought" claims is by selection effect a self-maintaining system, so the question "ought there be self-maintaining systems?" is asked only from within the class whose existence it questions (§3). Third, "ought F for agent S" identifies a conditional necessity-relation between F and S's persistence, with explicit extensions for non-necessary but persistence-relevant actions (§4). The result is dissolution rather than reduction: the gap is not bridged but shown to be an artefact of misapplied universal-scope semantics. The account is positioned against naturalistic moral realism (§7.1), constitutivism (§7.2), evolutionary ethics (§7.3), and error theory (§7.4), and concludes with explicit scope limitations including computational intractability, the dark-room limit, inter-agent normativity, and counterfactual ought-claims (§8). The dissolution claim is bounded: it resolves the core is-ought problem and grounds a tight epistemic imperative; it does not deliver a complete normative theory.

1. The Problem and Its Mischaracterization

1.1 Hume's argument

In A Treatise of Human Nature (Book III, Part I, §I), Hume observes that moral writers proceed from "is" propositions to "ought" propositions without explicating the inferential step, and concludes that the transition requires explanation no valid deductive inference supplies from descriptive premises alone.

The claim has a precise logical structure. It concerns deductive entailment between propositions of distinct syntactic types: indicative (descriptive) and normative (prescriptive). The claim is not metaphysical (about the nature of value), epistemological (about how value is known), or motivational (about how value moves to action). It is a claim about formal derivability.

1.2 The standard reading

In post-Humean meta-ethics, the gap has typically been read as an ontological claim about a categorical distinction between two types of fact (descriptive and normative) corresponding to two types of property (natural and non-natural). This reading is reinforced by Moore's open-question argument (Principia Ethica, 1903), which appears to show that no proposed naturalistic identity for "good" closes the conceptual gap: for any candidate property P, the question "is P actually good?" remains substantively open.

The standard reading generates an apparent trilemma: accept a non-natural moral realism with its attendant epistemological difficulties; an error theory denying the existence of moral facts (Mackie 1977); or non-cognitivism on which moral utterances are not truth-apt (Ayer 1936; Stevenson 1944).

1.3 The mischaracterization

The standard reading conflates two distinct claims:

(D) From descriptive premises alone, no normative conclusion follows by valid deductive inference. [Hume's claim]

(O) Normative claims pick out properties or facts of a categorically different kind than descriptive claims. [Standard ontological reading]

(D) is a logical observation about derivability. (O) is a metaphysical thesis about types of property. (D) does not entail (O). One can grant (D) while denying (O), provided one can show that the appearance of categorical distinction is generated by semantic structure rather than by ontological difference.

This paper grants (D) and rejects (O). The argument has three components, developed in §§2–4.

2. The Semantic Structure of "Ought"

2.1 "Ought" as a regulatory operator

In ordinary usage, "ought" claims have the form S ought to F, where S is an agent and F an action or state. The semantic content is regulatory: it evaluates or directs S's behavior with respect to a target.

Proposition 2.1. The semantic content of "S ought to F" presupposes (i) an agent S with goals or persistence-conditions, and (ii) a relation between F and those goals or conditions.

Without (i) or (ii), the claim has the surface form of an "ought" claim but lacks semantic content. Compare:

  • "You ought to eat to live." [agent: you; goal: to live; F: eating; well-formed]
  • "The asteroid ought to collide with Earth." [no agent or goals; ill-formed unless the asteroid is anthropomorphised or an implicit observer-frame supplied]
  • "The universe ought to exist." [no agent; no goal-relative frame; semantically empty unless a theistic or anthropic frame is supplied]

2.2 The type-error argument

Consider the question: "What is north of the North Pole?" The grammatical structure is well-formed. "North of" is a relational direction operator; "the North Pole" is a referring expression. Yet the question is not answerable, not because the answer is unknown, but because "north of" is undefined at the pole. The question is a type error in the geometry of the sphere.

The analogous claim for "ought":

Proposition 2.2. "Ought" is undefined outside the domain of agents with persistence-conditions. Questions of the form "ought there be X?" asked without specifying a referent agent or evaluative frame are type-errored, not false.

This is the first dissolutional move. Universal-scope "ought" questions ("ought there be a universe?", "ought there be life?") are not questions whose answers are hidden or contested. They are questions whose presuppositions fail. The grammatical surface obscures the semantic ill-formedness.

2.3 Comparison to existing semantic accounts

The agent-relative semantics here has antecedents in the literature but is distinct in its precise claim.

Anscombe (1958) argues that the moral "ought" lost coherence with the decline of theological frameworks that grounded its authority, and proposes restricting ethics to virtue concepts. The present account agrees that universal-scope "ought" requires a referent frame but does not require theological or virtue-theoretic grounding; the persistence-conditions of agents themselves supply the referent.

Foot (1958, 2001) argues that moral evaluation is a species of "natural goodness" tied to the form of life of the evaluated organism. The present account preserves this insight at a more general level: "ought" is keyed to the persistence-conditions of any self-maintaining system, not specifically to species-typical forms of life.

Stevenson (1944), Ayer (1936) hold emotivist or non-cognitivist views on which moral utterances are not truth-apt. The present account rejects this: properly-framed "ought" claims (with explicit agent and persistence frame) are truth-apt; their truth conditions are facts about persistence-relevance.

3. The Persistence Tautology

3.1 The selection effect

Proposition 3.1 (Persistence Tautology). Any system that does not maintain the conditions of its own persistence ceases to exist as a referent in subsequent time-steps. The class of observable systems at time t is the class of systems that have maintained their persistence-conditions up to t.

This is not a normative claim. It is a logical consequence of what "persistence" and "existence as observable" mean. It functions as a selection principle on the space of systems.

3.2 The asker is the answerer

Any agent capable of formulating the question "ought there be self-maintaining systems?" is itself a self-maintaining system. This is not contingent on the agent's biology; it is constitutive of being an agent in the formal sense (an entity capable of formulating claims).

Proposition 3.2. The set of askers of universal-scope "ought" questions is a strict subset of the set of self-maintaining systems. No system that fails to maintain itself is in a position to question whether it should maintain itself.

The structure is analogous to anthropic reasoning in cosmology: questions about why the universe permits observers are asked only by observers, and the existence of the question presupposes the conditions of its asking.

3.3 Constitutive vs. evaluative response to the selection objection

Objection. This is a mere selection effect; it does not show that persistence is good, only that non-persistence eliminates evaluators.

Response. The objection presupposes the standard reading (O). Once (O) is rejected and "ought" is recognised as agent-relative, the demand to show that persistence is good in a frame-independent sense is itself a type error. There is no frame-independent "good." For any specific agent S, the question "is persistence good for S?" has a frame: S's own persistence-conditions. The answer is constitutive: persistence is the precondition of any "good for S" being instantiable.

This is dissolution, not reduction. The framework does not derive a normative conclusion from a descriptive premise. It identifies the appearance of such a derivation as an artefact of treating "ought" as if it had universal-scope semantics it does not have.

4. The Identity Claim

4.1 Core identity

Proposition 4.1. For a self-maintaining system S and an action F, where F is necessary for S's persistence over interval Δt:
Ought(S, F) ⟺ [ ¬F → ¬∃S(t + Δt) ]

That is: "S ought to F" is equivalent to the conditional that S's not-F-ing causes S's non-persistence over Δt.

4.2 Scope and extensions

The identity in 4.1 captures strictly necessary persistence-relevant actions. It does not capture, without extension:

(a) Probabilistically relevant actions. Actions that increase or decrease persistence probability without strict necessity. Extension: replace the strict conditional with a probabilistic conditional and replace bare persistence with expected persistence-utility over relevant intervals.

(b) Flourishing-beyond-survival. Actions that improve persistence-quality (resource margins, capacity, resilience) without being strictly necessary for bare persistence. Extension: include conditions on persistence-quality, not only persistence-existence.

(c) Supererogatory acts. Actions that exceed what is strictly required of S. The framework treats these as actions whose connection to S's persistence-conditions is weak or absent at the individual level; their "ought" status (if any) requires inter-agent extension. The framework does not deliver a closed criterion for the supererogation threshold (§8.6).

(d) Counterfactual ought-claims. "S ought to have F'd" where S did not F. The framework handles these as evaluations against S's past persistence-conditions. The semantics extends straightforwardly; the epistemology of accessing past conditions is non-trivial.

4.3 Why this is not reduction

Reduction would require translating "ought" claims into "is" claims via a bridging definition: "S ought to F" means "F is necessary for S's persistence." Reduction is then vulnerable to the open-question objection: "yes, F is necessary for persistence, but is it good?"

The dissolution claim is structurally different. It denies the cogency of the open-question objection in this context. Once the agent-relative semantics of "ought" is recognised, the question "is persistence-necessity good?" has no frame-independent referent. The question is type-errored at the same level as "what is north of the North Pole?"

Moore's open-question argument retains force against reductive naturalism that aims to translate "good" into a natural property while preserving universal-scope semantics. It loses force against an account that denies the universal-scope semantics from the outset.

5. Epistemic Fidelity and the Cost of Misalignment

5.1 The cognitive-load asymmetry

For an agent S that holds both a true representation T and a competing false representation F, deploying F in communication or reasoning imposes higher cognitive cost than deploying T. This is empirically established across three decades of deception research:

  • Reaction-time penalty of approximately 200 to 300 milliseconds for deceptive responses relative to truthful responses (cognitive-load deception literature, principally Vrij, Walczyk and collaborators).
  • Elevated activation in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and inferior frontal gyrus during deception in fMRI studies (multiple replicated findings).
  • The basis of cognitive-load lie-detection methods (unexpected questions, reverse-order recall, dual-task interference), which operationalize the asymmetry as a measurement procedure.

The mechanism: deception requires inhibition of the prepotent truthful response, generation of a plausible alternative, and ongoing monitoring of consistency. Truth-telling requires only retrieval.

5.2 The free-energy framework

At a higher level of theoretical abstraction, the cognitive-load asymmetry expresses within variational free-energy minimization (Friston 2010, with subsequent developments). Agents minimize divergence between their internal generative model and the sensory evidence they receive. Maintaining a model that misaligns with evidence imposes a free-energy cost the agent must either compensate (additional cognitive resources) or resolve (model update).

Status of the free-energy framework: a productive theoretical research program with substantial uptake in cognitive neuroscience; not a fully settled physical principle. The present account uses it as theoretical framing for the cognitive-load asymmetry and does not depend on its strong ontological readings.

5.3 The persistence connection

For an agent operating in an environment with non-zero variance and finite resources, sustained misalignment between internal model and external reality degrades prediction accuracy and increases the rate of costly errors. Over time, this reduces persistence probability.

Proposition 5.1. In environments with variance V > 0 and resource constraints R < ∞, sustained model-reality misalignment in agent S monotonically reduces P(persist(S, t + Δt)) for Δt sufficiently large.

The qualification matters: in the limit V → 0 (the dark-room limit), false models persist without disconfirmation, and the cost of misalignment is not paid. This is a known boundary condition of the framework (§8.2).

6. The Epistemic Imperative

From §5: for agents in normal environments (V > 0, R < ∞), maintaining accurate models reduces cognitive load and improves persistence probability. The "ought" associated with this is:

Proposition 6.1 (Epistemic Imperative). For S in normal environments, S ought to minimize divergence between internal model and external reality.

This follows from Proposition 4.1 and Proposition 5.1 under the relevant environmental conditions. The derivation is tight: the connection between model fidelity and persistence is structural, mediated by the cost of error.

The framework's positive normative output is this single imperative. It does not output:

  • A theory of inter-agent normativity (justice, rights, cooperation; see §8.4).
  • A closed criterion for supererogation (see §4.2c, §8.6).
  • A solution to trolley-type dilemmas, which turn on inter-agent normativity not developed here.
  • A complete decision procedure for moral dilemmas (see §8.1).

These are scope limitations of the present framework's normative output, not defects of the dissolution argument as such.

7. Positioning Against Alternatives

7.1 Cornell naturalistic moral realism

Boyd (1988), Brink (1989), Sturgeon (1985), and Railton (1986) advance naturalistic moral realism: moral properties are natural properties (broadly construed), and moral facts are facts about those properties.

The dissolution account agrees that "ought" claims, properly framed, are facts about agent-persistence-conditions in the natural world. It differs in two ways:

(a) Cornell realism typically retains universal-scope semantics for "good" and "right" and argues that these terms refer to natural properties via a causal-historical theory of reference (analogous to Kripke-Putnam for natural kinds). The dissolution account denies universal-scope semantics: "ought" is irreducibly agent-relative.

(b) Cornell realism is vulnerable to refined open-question objections (Horgan and Timmons 1991, "Moral Twin Earth"). The dissolution account is not vulnerable in the same way, because the open question is reframed as a type-error rather than treated as a substantive question about reference.

7.2 Constitutivism

Korsgaard (1996, 2009) derives normative conclusions from the constitutive aims of agency: to be an agent at all is to be committed to certain principles (the categorical imperative, in her Kantian reconstruction).

The dissolution account shares the structural move of grounding "ought" in conditions constitutive of agency. It differs in:

(a) The constitutive aim. Korsgaard locates it in the unity of agency and self-legislation of practical reason. The present account locates it in persistence under thermodynamic constraints.

(b) The normative content derived. Korsgaard derives Kantian universalizability. The present account derives only the epistemic imperative of §6.

(c) Scope of agents. Korsgaard's account targets specifically rational agents. The present account targets any self-maintaining system; the derivation of normative content scales with the complexity of the agent's persistence-relevant model.

7.3 Evolutionary ethics

Ruse (1986), Wilson (1975), and others argue that moral intuitions and norms are products of evolutionary pressures on cooperative behavior. The dissolution account agrees with the causal claim (moral capacities have evolutionary origins) but distinguishes:

(a) The evolutionary account is a genealogy of moral intuitions; it does not settle questions about their normative authority.

(b) The dissolution account is not a genealogy. It is a semantic and metaphysical account of what "ought" claims pick out. The two are compatible at different explanatory levels.

(c) The dissolution account does not commit to the claim that all moral intuitions track persistence-relevant facts. Some intuitions may be evolutionary byproducts that misfire in modern environments; the framework supplies a basis for evaluating which.

7.4 Mackie's error theory

Mackie (1977) holds that moral claims commit to objective values that do not exist, and concludes that all moral claims are false.

The dissolution account denies Mackie's first premise. Moral claims, properly framed, do not commit to frame-independent objective values. They commit to agent-relative persistence-conditions, which exist. Mackie's error theory presupposes the standard universal-scope reading of "ought" the dissolution account rejects.

8. Scope, Open Questions, Boundary Conditions

The following are explicitly unsettled or unaddressed by the present framework. They are flagged, not concealed.

8.1 Computational intractability

Even granting that "ought" facts for agent S are determinate (given S's persistence-conditions and environment), computing them in real time may exceed S's resources. The framework identifies what S ought to approximate; it does not provide a tractable algorithm. This is the bounded-rationality problem (Simon 1956) extended to ethics.

8.2 The dark-room limit

In environments with V → 0 and unlimited resources, false models persist without disconfirmation. The cost of misalignment is not paid, and the epistemic imperative loses its grounding. The framework's normative output is conditional on V > 0 and R < ∞. The dark-room case is not refuted; it is identified as the regime where the framework does not bind.

8.3 Phenomenal consciousness

The framework supports a functional account of valence (positive and negative affect as signals about persistence-trajectory) but does not explain the phenomenal character of these states. The hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers 1995) is not addressed and is not claimed to be.

8.4 Inter-agent normativity

The framework grounds individual-scale "ought" claims. It does not develop an account of:

  • Justice (distributive and procedural).
  • Rights (claim-rights, liberty-rights, immunities).
  • Conflict resolution under incompatible persistence-claims between agents.
  • Aggregation across persons.
  • Whether cooperation is normatively required, optional, or context-dependent for self-maintaining systems in multi-agent environments.

These are core domains of normative theory. The dissolution account, as presently developed, restricts its primary claim to the dissolution of the core is-ought distinction. Inter-agent normativity is flagged as unsolved and is treated as a domain for future work, not as a settled output of the framework.

8.5 Counterfactual and historical ought-claims

"S ought to have F'd" where S did not F requires evaluation against S's past persistence-conditions. The semantics extends straightforwardly. The epistemology of accessing past conditions is non-trivial and may yield underdetermined answers.

8.6 Supererogation

Acts that exceed what is required of S are not captured by the strict-necessity identity in §4.1. The framework can extend to include them via persistence-quality considerations (§4.2b), but the threshold between required and supererogatory remains underdetermined.

8.7 Population ethics

Questions about whether one ought to bring new agents into existence (procreation, antinatalism) require an account of how persistence-claims aggregate across actual and potential agents. The framework does not currently supply one.

8.8 Status of the underlying theoretical commitments

The framework's tighter results (§§2–4) depend on the semantic analysis of "ought" and the persistence tautology. These are defensible on their own terms. The framework's looser results (§5 and the imperative derived in §6) depend additionally on the free-energy principle as a productive research program rather than as a settled physical principle. The dissolution claim itself does not depend on the looser results; the epistemic imperative of §6 does.

9. Conclusion

The is-ought distinction, as Hume formulated it, is a correct observation about formal deductive entailment between propositions of distinct syntactic types. It is not, as commonly read, an ontological claim about a categorical gap between fact and value.

The apparent gap dissolves when the semantic structure of "ought" is correctly identified. "Ought" is an agent-relative regulatory operator. Its content presupposes an agent with persistence-conditions. Outside this presupposition, "ought" claims are type-errored, not false. Within this presupposition, "ought" claims pick out conditional necessity-relations between actions and persistence-conditions.

The apparent gap was generated by treating "ought" as if it had universal-scope semantics. Once universal-scope is dropped and agent-relativity is recognised, the gap is not bridged but shown to be an artefact of misapplied grammar.

The dissolution claim is bounded. It resolves the core is-ought distinction and grounds an epistemic imperative tightly. It does not settle inter-agent normativity, supererogation, population ethics, or the phenomenal character of moral experience. These remain open and are explicitly flagged as such.

References

Anscombe, G. E. M. (1958). Modern Moral Philosophy. Philosophy 33(124), 1–19.

Ayer, A. J. (1936). Language, Truth and Logic. Gollancz.

Boyd, R. (1988). How to Be a Moral Realist. In G. Sayre-McCord (ed.), Essays on Moral Realism. Cornell University Press.

Brink, D. (1989). Moral Realism and the Foundations of Ethics. Cambridge University Press.

Chalmers, D. (1995). Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness. Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 200–219.

Foot, P. (1958). Moral Beliefs. Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 59, 83–104.

Foot, P. (2001). Natural Goodness. Oxford University Press.

Friston, K. (2010). The Free-Energy Principle: A Unified Brain Theory? Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11(2), 127–138.

Horgan, T. and Timmons, M. (1991). New Wave Moral Realism Meets Moral Twin Earth. Journal of Philosophical Research 16, 447–465.

Hume, D. (1739). A Treatise of Human Nature. Book III, Part I, §I.

Korsgaard, C. (1996). The Sources of Normativity. Cambridge University Press.

Korsgaard, C. (2009). Self-Constitution: Agency, Identity, and Integrity. Oxford University Press.

Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong. Penguin.

Moore, G. E. (1903). Principia Ethica. Cambridge University Press.

Railton, P. (1986). Moral Realism. Philosophical Review 95(2), 163–207.

Ruse, M. (1986). Taking Darwin Seriously. Blackwell.

Simon, H. (1956). Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment. Psychological Review 63(2), 129–138.

Stevenson, C. L. (1944). Ethics and Language. Yale University Press.

Sturgeon, N. (1985). Moral Explanations. In D. Copp and D. Zimmerman (eds.), Morality, Reason and Truth. Rowman and Littlefield.

Vrij, A., Fisher, R., Mann, S., and Leal, S. (multiple studies, 2003–2012). Cognitive-load approach to deception detection.

Walczyk, J., Roper, K., Seemann, E., and Humphrey, A. (multiple studies, 2003–2014). Reaction-time asymmetries in deception.

Wilson, E. O. (1975). Sociobiology: The New Synthesis. Harvard University Press.

Written by Andraž. Developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic). The dissolution argument, the persistence-tautology grounding, and the agent-relative semantic framework originate with the author across earlier working papers; this paper is the consolidated statement.

entry.title: In parts of the universe where self-maintaining replicators arise..
entry.content: In parts of the universe where self-maintaining replicators arise, selection tends to produce systems that build increasingly accurate and compressed models of their local environment; in that limited sense, the universe contains processes that come to “understand” other parts of the universe.

entry.title: Casualty Analysis: Direct and Indirect Death Tolls in Gaza vs. Ukraine (April 2026)
entry.content:
Data Analysis Report

The Arithmetic of Erasure

Gaza Strip and Ukraine  /  April 2026  / 
Raw casualty data from Gaza and Ukraine offers a measurable basis for comparison, but only if presented with precision. This report distinguishes throughout between confirmed figures (reported by health ministries and independently verified by UN bodies) and projections (peer-reviewed estimates incorporating indirect mortality).
Confirmed — reported and independently verified
Projected — peer-reviewed estimate with inherent uncertainty
Section 01

Gaza: confirmed and estimated toll

As of mid-April 2026, the Gaza Health Ministry has published named records for over 72,000 Palestinians killed since October 7, 2023. Both US and Israeli intelligence have assessed these figures as generally reliable. UN agencies note the count is likely an undercount, as it excludes those dying from the war-induced collapse of medical, water, and food systems.

Confirmed
72,300+
Direct deaths, named and recorded
Confirmed
~21,300
Children killed (approx. 2% of Gaza minors)
Projected
186,000+
Total mortality including indirect deaths
Confirmed
88%
Population internally displaced (~1.9 million)
The indirect toll: Beyond direct strikes, thousands are dying from war-induced causes: famine resulting from aid restrictions, deaths from lack of insulin or dialysis, and infectious disease outbreaks caused by destruction of sewage and water systems. These deaths are real but harder to count with precision.
On the 186,000+ projection: This figure originates from a peer-reviewed analysis in The Lancet, applying a standard public health multiplier to account for indirect deaths that do not appear in hospital records. It is a credible estimate, not a confirmed count. The true figure lies somewhere between the confirmed 72,300 and this upper projection.
Section 02

Gaza vs. Ukraine: a proportional comparison

This comparison isolates one victim population from each conflict: Palestinian civilians in Gaza, and Ukrainians (civilian and military) killed in Russia's invasion. It does not compare the conflicts as wholes. The Russian military death toll alone runs into the hundreds of thousands, and is excluded here.

Metric
Gaza Strip (2.5 years)
Ukraine (4 years)
Confirmed direct deaths
~72,300
Palestinians killed
~70,000
Civilian and military Ukrainians
Total est. deaths (incl. indirect)
~186,000
Projected
100,000 – 140,000
Projected
Proportional loss (using projections)
1 in 12
people
1 in 300
people
Civilian share of deaths
~80% civilian
Source: OHCHR
~20% civilian
Source: OHCHR
Ability to flee
Severely restricted
Blockade in effect
High
Millions displaced to EU
On Ukraine figures: OHCHR verified approximately 15,172 Ukrainian civilian deaths and President Zelenskyy confirmed 55,000 Ukrainian military deaths (February 2026), for a confirmed total of roughly 70,000 on the Ukrainian side. CSIS estimates military deaths could reach 140,000. The proportional comparison uses mid-range estimates throughout.
Section 03

What the data shows and does not show

The confirmed numbers establish several things clearly: the scale of civilian death in Gaza is proportionally without recent parallel; the civilian share of deaths is dramatically higher than in Ukraine; and the population has no meaningful ability to flee. These are measurable facts.

What the data does not settle by itself is the question of intent. Whether the pattern of destruction constitutes a deliberate policy of elimination is a legal determination, one currently before the International Court of Justice. That question requires evidentiary standards beyond casualty statistics alone.

What is not in dispute: the humanitarian outcome is catastrophic by any comparative measure, and the structural conditions including blockade, destruction of civilian infrastructure, and restriction of medical supplies have materially contributed to the death toll beyond direct military strikes.

Summary: what the numbers establish

Confirmed

~72,300 Palestinians killed directly, ~21,300 of them children (approximately 2% of Gaza's minors). 88% of the population displaced. Civilian share of deaths approximately 80%.

Projected (Lancet methodology)

Total mortality including indirect deaths likely exceeds 186,000, roughly 1 in 12 of Gaza's population, when accounting for deaths from infrastructure collapse, famine, and medical system failure.

Comparative finding

The proportional death toll in Gaza is dramatically higher than in Ukraine on a per-capita basis, and the civilian composition of those deaths is inverted. These are the facts the data supports. Legal and political conclusions beyond this require separate analysis.

Sources
  • Gaza Health Ministry (MoH) — direct casualty records, named database of 72,004 individuals (March 2026)
  • UNICEF State of Palestine Situation Update (February 2026) — children killed figure (~21,289)
  • UN OHCHR — civilian casualty verification, Ukraine and Gaza
  • The Lancet (January 2025, peer-reviewed) — indirect mortality projection, 186,000+ estimate
  • CSIS / Russia Matters — Ukrainian military casualty estimates (January to March 2026)
  • Zelenskyy (February 2026) — confirmed Ukrainian military deaths (55,000)
  • UNRWA Situation Report #216 (April 2026) — displacement and infrastructure data
